META.subtitleDoc: CBE Phenomenon-Driven Lesson Sequence — Sub-Strand 3.1 (16 Lessons)

UNIT.subject: Core Mathematics
UNIT.totalDuration: 16 lessons × 40 minutes = 640 minutes total (15 teaching lessons plus 1 summative assessment lesson)
UNIT.content:
• Collection of Data
• Frequency distribution table
• Mean, Mode and Median of grouped and ungrouped data
• Representation of Data
• Interpretation of Data
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) collect data from real-life sources,
b) draw a frequency distribution table for grouped and ungrouped data,
c) determine mean, mode and median of grouped and ungrouped data,
d) represent data using histograms and frequency polygons,
e) interpret data from histograms and frequency polygons,
f) promote data collection, organisation and representation for informed decision making.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Critical thinking and problem solving: the learner uses the histograms and frequency polygons to examine data and make conclusions.
• Self-Efficacy: the learner discusses with peers the meaning of the term data and explores data sources.
• Digital literacy: the learner uses digital devices to draw histograms and frequency polygons to make conclusions.
• Communication and collaboration: learner presents and shares findings from data to different groups of people such as school administrators, parents or local community leaders.
UNIT.values:
• Integrity: the learner collects and records data accurately.
• Unity: the learner works in groups and uses collected data to draw histograms and frequency polygons.
• Love: the learner is considerate of the other as they discuss in pairs and identify the modal class for grouped data.
UNIT.sep:
• Asking Questions and Defining Problems: students ask questions about why pedestrians cross at undesignated points and what data would answer them.
• Planning and Carrying Out Investigations: students design and run a tally survey of crossing points and pedestrian behaviour along a road near school.
• Analyzing and Interpreting Data: students build frequency tables, compute mean, median and mode, and read histograms and frequency polygons.
• Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking: students use grouped-data formulas, class widths, frequency density and spreadsheets or calculators.
• Constructing Explanations: students use data evidence to explain patterns and defend recommendations.
• Engaging in Argument from Evidence: students critique which measure of average best represents the data and justify it.
• Developing and Using Models: students revise a class data model (table, graph, summary measures) after each lesson.
• Obtaining, Evaluating and Communicating Information: students present findings to the school administration or community leaders.
UNIT.pcis:
• Life Skills (Decision Making): the learner makes informed decisions from data interpretation from histograms and frequency polygons.
• Parental Engagement and Empowerment: the learner seeks support and guidance from parents or guardians to collect, organise and present data on an identified situation in the school or community.
• Road Safety (link to the suggested data context): pedestrian crossing point data is used to argue for safer roads.
UNIT.careers:
• Statistician / Data Analyst (Kenya National Bureau of Statistics): collects and analyses census and survey data.
• Transport and Road Safety Planner (NTSA, KeNHA): uses crossing and traffic data to place footbridges and zebra crossings.
• Agricultural Extension Officer: analyses maize and tea yield data from Kericho and the Rift Valley.
• Public Health Officer: uses data to track clinic attendance and disease trends.
• Economist, Actuary and Data Scientist: use data to guide policy, insurance and technology (M-Pesa, Safaricom analytics).
UNIT.focus: Learners investigate a real road-safety problem near their school by collecting, organising, summarising and graphing their own data. They move from raw tallies to frequency tables, measures of central tendency, histograms and frequency polygons, and finally to evidence-based recommendations. Each lesson follows Predict, Observe, Explain, DQB and Model Building so that understanding of the anchoring phenomenon grows cumulatively.
UNIT.phenomenon: Along a busy road near the school (for example Thika Road in Nairobi, Mombasa Road, or the Kisumu-Kakamega highway), a county road safety officer says: 'The average distance between pedestrian crossing points is only about 400 m, so the road is well served.' Yet learners see pedestrians, including school children, dashing across at undesignated spots, and a local matatu driver says most near-misses happen in just one stretch. Learners tally the crossing points and pedestrians themselves and find that the mean looks reassuring while the raw data show a few very long gaps. The puzzle: how can an average say the road is safe while the data show danger in particular places, and which statistical tools reveal the true story?
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• Two Grade 10 classes in Nakuru both have a mean KCSE-style mock score of 62%, but one class has scores bunched together and the other has a wide spread; which class needs more teacher support?
• A maize farmer in Trans-Nzoia records bags harvested per acre over 40 plots; the mean is pulled up by a few exceptionally good plots, so the median tells a different story.
• A mandazi vendor at Kisumu bus park records daily sales for a month; grouping the sales into classes reveals the busiest sales band that the raw list hides.
• Kenyan marathon runners (such as Eliud Kipchoge's training group in Kaptagat) record weekly distances; a histogram shows the typical training band better than a list of numbers.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: How can we use data from our own road to show where pedestrians are really at risk, and why does one average not tell the whole story?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS:
1. What is statistics?
2. How do we represent data?
3. How do we use statistics in day-to-day life?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1: Predict whether the road near school is safe from the officer's claim; study the claim, the near-miss log and three source cards (survey, observation, records); choose a source for each question about the road; start the DQB and draw an initial model.
Lesson 2: Define data and statistics in learners' own words by sorting facts and figures from conclusions; sort and star the DQB questions; extend the model with a plan for finding out.
Lesson 3: Collect data on the gaps between pedestrian crossing points using tallies; build a frequency distribution table for the 20 ungrouped gap lengths and check the totals (20 gaps, 8,000 m).
Lesson 4: Build the frequency table of pedestrians crossing at undesignated spots in each gap (182 in total); notice that the six large counts match the six long gaps.
Lesson 5: Determine the mean and mode of ungrouped data; confirm that the officer's mean of 400 m is true arithmetic and that the mode (200 m) is quite different.
Lesson 6: Determine the median and range of ungrouped data; compare mean, median and mode to test the officer's 'average' claim and discuss which measure best represents the data.
Lesson 7: Group the collected data (for example gaps between crossing points) into appropriate classes; draw a grouped frequency table and identify the modal class in pairs.
Lesson 8: Estimate the mean of grouped data using class midpoints; compare with the ungrouped mean.
Lesson 9: Estimate the median of grouped data using cumulative frequency; compare with ungrouped results and revise the class model.
Lesson 10: Draw a histogram with equal class widths from the collected data; observe how the long gaps stand out from the short ones.
Lesson 11: Draw histograms with unequal class widths using frequency density; link the long gaps to the pedestrians and the near-miss log.
Lesson 12: Draw frequency polygons by hand from class midpoints and read their shape.
Lesson 13: Draw frequency polygons with digital devices or spreadsheets; compare polygons from different roads and make conclusions.
Lesson 14: Interpret histograms and polygons together with the measures and tables, write the final explanation of the phenomenon and redraw the model.
Lesson 15: Make informed recommendations, present findings to the school administration, parents or community leaders, and complete the final model and DQB review for the project.
Lesson 16: Summative assessment for the whole sub-strand: a new question about the same road (pedestrians per gap) assessed across all the KICD outcomes in the five-phase structure, alongside the Final Explanation.

LESSONS.title: Is the Road Really Well Served? The Claim, the Evidence and Where Data Come From
LESSONS.aresKeywords: data, statistics, survey, observation, records, undesignated crossing, designated crossing point, gap, average, near-miss, Driving Question Board

slo.purpose: Launch the Thika Road phenomenon. Learners meet the county Road Safety Officer's claim that the average gap between crossing points is about 400 m, so the road is well served. They compare it with what they see at the school gate and with Mzee Otieno's remark that most near-misses happen in one stretch, name three sources of data and plan which source could test the claim. They also draw a first model of the road.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (1) name and describe three sources of data (surveys, observation, records) and give a Thika Road example of each; (2) state what an undesignated crossing is; (3) choose a safe, suitable data source for a question about the road and name one thing that could go wrong; (4) explain why the officer's average of 400 m might not tell the whole story. Learners do no calculations in this lesson.
slo.skills: Making predictions from partial evidence; asking questions from a puzzling phenomenon; planning an investigation (what to measure, how, and with which source); communicating reasoning in pairs and to the class; drawing a first model of the road.
slo.attitudes: Integrity (the learner collects and records data accurately, as they plan how to do so); Unity (the learner works in groups to plan the data collection); Love (the learner is considerate of others when discussing). Core competencies: Self-Efficacy (the learner discusses with peers the meaning of the term data and explores data sources); Critical thinking and problem solving. PCIs: Road safety; Life Skills (Decision Making).
slo.keyInquiry: 1. What is statistics? 2. How do we represent data? 3. How do we use statistics in day-to-day life? (Lesson 1 focuses on question 1 and opens questions 2 and 3 on the DQB.)
slo.purposeInStoryline: This lesson launches the storyline. Learners accept that the officer's mean of 400 m is arithmetically true but suspect it may be incomplete. The Driving Question Board (DQB) is started here and the first model is drawn here; both are revisited in every later lesson. Lesson 2 then names data and statistics in the learners' own words and turns their questions into a plan, and Lesson 3 starts the counting.
slo.safetyNotes: No learner goes onto Thika Road in this lesson. All work is in the classroom, using only the stated claim and the near-miss log. When the real survey is done later, it must be done with Mwalimu Wanjiru and parent or guardian volunteers on a safe footpath, never on the carriageway, and learners must never cross at undesignated spots to count. Treat pedestrian and near-miss stories sensitively, as some learners or relatives may have been involved in road accidents.

LESSONS.overview: Mwalimu Wanjiru opens by reading the county Road Safety Officer Ms Halima Abdi's statement about the 8,000 m stretch of Thika Road from Roysambu stage towards Ruiru: it has 21 designated crossing points and the average distance between them is about 400 m, so the road is well served. Learners recall what they see at Ruaraka Hills Secondary School's gate each morning, with children dashing across away from zebra crossings and footbridges (undesignated crossings), and hear Mzee Otieno, a matatu driver, say that most of his near-misses happen in just one stretch. In the Predict phase learners commit to a prediction on a Predict Card. In the Observe phase groups study the officer's statement, a log of 12 near-misses and three source cards (survey, observation, records). In the Explain phase pairs choose the best source for each question about the road and say what could go wrong. The class starts the Driving Question Board with one question per learner, and learners draw an initial model of the road to be revised in later lessons. The second half of this topic is Lesson 2, where learners define data and statistics. Pacing for a 40-minute period: Predict 5 min, Observe 14 min, Explain 8 min, Driving Question Board 4 min, Model Building 9 min.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners meet the phenomenon. Mwalimu Wanjiru reads aloud, as a county notice: 'On the 8,000 m stretch of Thika Road from Roysambu stage towards Ruiru there are 21 designated crossing points (zebra crossings and footbridges). The average distance between crossing points is about 400 m, so the road is well served.' (Ms Halima Abdi, County Road Safety Officer). Learners then picture the school gate, which is at the 4,000 m mark, on a weekday morning at 6:30-7:30 am: matatus, boda bodas, and learners and workers dashing across away from the crossings. Mzee Otieno's remark is read: 'Most of my near-misses happen in just one stretch.' Individually, for 3 minutes, learners write on a Predict Card: (a) Is the road near our school safe for pedestrians? Circle: Safe / Not safe / Safe in some places and not in others. (b) One reason from the officer's claim or from what you have seen. (c) One thing you would need to know to be sure. They then share in pairs (Think-Pair-Share), and the class makes a tally on the board of the three choices.
framework.teacherMoves: Read the notice slowly, then say: 'Ms Abdi is not careless or dishonest. Let us treat her statement as something we can test.' Ask: 'Picture our gate at 6:45 in the morning. What do you see?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Cold-call 3 learners for what they see, e.g. 'Achieng, what do you see at our gate?', and then read Mzee Otieno's remark. Distribute Predict Cards and give 3 minutes of silent writing. Move around reading cards; select 2 contrasting predictions without naming the writers. Say: 'Turn to your partner and share your prediction and your reason. Your partner should say whether the reason convinces them.' Then take the hand tally on the three choices and record it on the board. Cold-call 4 pairs for the 'what would you need to know' item and write the answers on the board, unedited. Do NOT say whether anyone is right. Say: 'Today we will not decide who is right. We will work out what data could settle it.' Do not introduce any calculation.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain with Think-Pair-Share. Committing to a prediction before any instruction exposes learners' existing ideas, in particular that an average of 400 m means every part of the road is equally served. Writing 'what I would need to know' moves learners from opinion to the need for evidence, which motivates the idea of data.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) learners who write 'Safe in some places and not in others' or who mention uneven spacing show early awareness of spread; (2) learners who accept the average as proof of safety hold the misconception that one average describes the whole road; note names and revisit in Lesson 5. (3) Predict Cards that give a reason that draws on evidence (the officer's figure, the gate, Mzee Otieno) rather than just opinion. (4) The 'what I need to know' items that mention counting pedestrians, measuring distances or asking drivers show readiness to think about data. Record the tally of predictions to compare with at the end of the unit.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of four (roles: Achieng - recorder for the data sources, Kiprop - reader of the cards, Njeri - sketcher, and one spokesperson). Each group receives three printed or board-copied items. Item 1 is the officer's claim with the facts: 8,000 m, 21 crossing points, about 400 m average. Item 2 is the near-miss log kept for one week by matatu drivers led by Mzee Otieno: 12 near-misses were recorded; the drivers say most happened in one stretch around the school gate (the full breakdown of where they happened is withheld until a later lesson). Item 3 is a set of three Source Cards: Survey (asking people questions, e.g. asking 30 learners how they get to school and where they cross), Observation (watching and counting, e.g. standing safely at a footpath and tallying pedestrians crossing away from zebra crossings and measuring distance between crossing points with a trundle wheel or tape measure), and Records (information already written down, e.g. the matatu drivers' near-miss log, county road records, police accident records, school registers). Groups complete a table with three columns: 'Source', 'Thika Road example', 'What it could tell us about the officer's claim'. They also write what they notice about the near-miss log: what kind of information is it, who collected it, and what is missing. Groups also note a puzzle: 'The officer says well served, the driver says danger in one stretch. How can both be told by data?'
framework.teacherMoves: Before groups start, say: 'You are detectives. Every piece of information on your table is a clue.' Circulate and ask each group: 'Which of these clues did someone measure, which did someone ask, and which did someone write down?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. Prompt groups that stall: 'If you wanted to check whether the road is well served, would the officer's 400 m tell you where the gaps are long?' (do not answer it). Ask: 'What does the near-miss log tell us? What does it not tell us?' After 10 minutes, cold-call 3 groups to share one row of their table, e.g. 'Group 2, give us a survey example on Thika Road.' Use the discussion to clarify: a source gives data, and data can be gathered by asking, watching or looking at records. Note that the near-miss log has 12 entries, and ask: 'Is 12 a lot? What would you compare it with?' Accept all ideas and record them on the board under 'Observe: what we notice'. Introduce the term undesignated crossing: 'A pedestrian crossing the road away from a zebra crossing or footbridge.' Do not give pedestrian counts or gap lengths.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence table (claim-evidence-source analysis) with a gallery-style share. Sorting real clues into survey, observation and records builds the idea that data comes from different sources, each with different strengths. Asking what a source cannot tell us develops critical thinking about the quality of evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) groups correctly classify the near-miss log as records and counting pedestrians as observation; (2) groups give a Thika Road example for each source that is realistic and safe, e.g. asking learners and drivers (survey) rather than crossing the road; (3) groups notice that the near-miss log does not say where on the road each event happened or how many pedestrians cross; (4) at least one learner per group voices that the average 400 m does not show whether distances are equal. Use a checklist with the four indicators. If a group cannot classify the sources, ask them to say how each piece of information was obtained (asked, watched, or read).

framework.learnerExperience: Pairs take four question prompts and choose the best data source for each: (1) 'How would you find out how far apart the crossing points really are?' (2) 'How would you find out how many pedestrians cross away from the zebra crossings, and where?' (3) 'How would you find out whether near-misses cluster in one stretch?' (4) 'Who might disagree with our data, and why?' For each prompt the pair names the source (survey, observation or records), says why, and says what could go wrong (for example counting on only one morning, asking too few people, or a log that drivers kept for only one week). The class then notices that the officer's 400 m is itself a figure that came from data: the length of the road (8,000 m) and the number of crossing points (21).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'You chose observation. Where will you stand? How will you keep safe? On which day and time?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 4 pairs, one for each prompt, e.g. 'Kiprop and partner, which source for question 1, and why?' Challenge weak choices: 'Would asking people tell you how many metres apart the crossings are?' Highlight integrity: 'How do we make sure our tallies are honest and accurate?' Ask: 'Is the officer's 400 m data? Where did it come from?' Keep every plan safe: observation is done from a safe footpath with adults, never on the carriageway. Do not teach calculation of mean, median or mode; if asked, say 'We will test this in Lesson 5.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured pair talk with source-to-question matching. Choosing a source and naming its weakness builds early understanding of data quality and sampling, and links the abstract idea of data to a concrete decision about their own road.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) a sensible match of source to question (observation for counting pedestrians and measuring gaps, records for near-misses, survey for opinions or habits); (2) at least one limitation named, such as a single morning or a small sample; (3) learners recognising that the officer's average is itself based on data; (4) plans that are safe and realistic. Quick check on a slip: 'Name one question about the road and the source you would use to answer it.'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners start the Driving Question Board. The driving question is placed at the top of a chart: 'How can we use data from our own road to show where pedestrians are really at risk, and why does one average not tell the whole story?' Three columns below carry the KICD key inquiry questions: 'What is statistics?', 'How do we represent data?', 'How do we use statistics in day-to-day life?' Each learner writes one question on a sticky note that arises from the phenomenon, for example 'Are the crossing points evenly spaced?', 'Where exactly do the near-misses happen?' or 'Can one number describe a whole road?', and posts it under the column it fits best or in a 'Not sure yet' area. Sorting and starring the questions is finished in Lesson 2.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'A good question is one that data can help us answer.' Model two examples on the board, one strong ('Where along the 8,000 m are the gaps between crossing points longest?') and one that needs rewording ('Is the officer bad?'), and ask learners to say what makes the difference. Give 2 minutes of silent writing. Invite 4 learners to post a note and read it aloud. Reword questions with the learner, not for them. Place the board where it stays visible during the unit and say: 'We will come back to this board in every lesson.' Do not promise answers yet.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board launch. Learners' own questions become the learning agenda, which gives them ownership and a visible record of growing understanding. Sorting under the three KICD key inquiry questions links their curiosity to the sub-strand outcomes.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) the proportion of notes that are testable by data rather than opinions; (2) notes that show curiosity about spread or location (for example 'Are all gaps the same length?'); (3) notes posted under a sensible KICD question. Notes that need rewording can be coached individually while others write. Keep a photograph or copy of the board.

framework.learnerExperience: Individually, learners draw an Initial Model on a sheet of paper or in the exercise book. They draw a line to represent the 8,000 m stretch of Thika Road from Roysambu stage towards Ruiru, mark the school gate at the 4,000 m mark, and place 21 small marks for crossing points in the way they think they are spaced (they may spread them evenly or not). They add where they think pedestrians cross away from the crossings and where near-misses happen, using arrows or shading. Beneath the drawing they write: (1) 'The officer's average of 400 m is ... ' (true / false / true but not enough, with a reason); (2) 'I think the data would show ...'; (3) 'Three things I want to find out.' Pairs compare models and mark one similarity and one difference. Learners keep the model in their books for revision in later lessons.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Draw what you think the road really looks like. There is no wrong model today, because this is a first idea we will test.' Remind learners the 400 m average is true as arithmetic: 8,000 m shared among the gaps does give about 400 m. Say: 'Her figure is true but may be incomplete. Show in your model whether the crossing points are evenly spaced or not.' Do not correct models. Circulate and ask: 'Why did you put the crossings there?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to describe their models in one sentence. Ask the class: 'How many models show all crossings evenly spaced? How many show clusters or long empty stretches?' Count hands and write the numbers on the board. Collect the Predict Cards and models for later comparison. Hand-off: 'Next lesson we put into words what data and statistics are, and decide which questions to investigate first.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Initial model drawing with pair comparison. Putting ideas into a spatial model forces learners to make their thinking about spacing and risk explicit, so that it can be revised against evidence as the unit proceeds. Comparing models reveals different assumptions to be tested.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) models that show uneven spacing of crossing points or clusters of pedestrians, showing an early grasp that an average hides variation; (2) models with evenly spaced crossings and a claim that the road is safe, indicating the misconception to address in Lessons 5 to 15; (3) a 'true but not enough' judgement with a reason; (4) 'things I want to find out' that refer to counts, distances or locations. Sort the models into three piles (even, clustered, unsure). Exit question: 'Name one source of data and one thing it could tell us about Thika Road.'

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, review the Predict Cards and initial models. How many learners predicted 'safe', 'not safe' and 'safe in some places'? Did learners treat Ms Abdi's claim respectfully as true but possibly incomplete? Which groups could match a data source to a question, and which confused survey, observation and records? Did the DQB notes include testable questions? Note any learner who was affected by road accidents and offer support. Check that safe arrangements with parent or guardian volunteers will be in place for any later data collection.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed the County Road Safety Officer's claim that the average distance between crossing points on the 8,000 m stretch of Thika Road is about 400 m (21 crossing points), and that this is true. We also saw learners crossing away from the crossings at our school gate, and we read the log of 12 near-misses kept by Mzee Otieno and other matatu drivers, who say most happen in one stretch.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned three sources of data: surveys (asking), observation (watching, counting and measuring) and records (information already written down). We learned that an undesignated crossing is a pedestrian crossing away from a zebra crossing or footbridge, and that each source has strengths and limits.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can explain that the officer's average of 400 m may be true but incomplete, because one number may not show whether the crossing points are evenly spaced or where pedestrians are at risk. To test the claim we need to collect our own data, choosing the source that best fits each question, safely and honestly.

LESSONS.title: What Are Data? What Is Statistics? Turning Our Questions into a Plan
LESSONS.aresKeywords: data, statistics, survey, observation, records, undesignated crossing, designated crossing point, gap, average, near-miss, Driving Question Board

slo.purpose: Learners put the terms data and statistics into their own words using Thika Road examples, separate facts and figures (data) from opinions and conclusions, finish the Driving Question Board by sorting and starring questions that data can answer, and extend their first model with a plan for how to find out.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (1) explain the meaning of the term data and of statistics, using 'data' as a plural; (2) tell a measured, counted or recorded figure from an opinion or a conclusion, and name the source each figure came from; (3) say how statistics is used in day-to-day life; (4) choose, from the Driving Question Board, three questions to investigate first. Learners do no calculations in this lesson.
slo.skills: Making predictions from partial evidence; asking questions from a puzzling phenomenon; planning an investigation (what to measure, how, and with which source); communicating reasoning in pairs and to the class; drawing a first model of the road.
slo.attitudes: Integrity (the learner collects and records data accurately, as they plan how to do so); Unity (the learner works in groups to plan the data collection); Love (the learner is considerate of others when discussing). Core competencies: Self-Efficacy (the learner discusses with peers the meaning of the term data and explores data sources); Critical thinking and problem solving. PCIs: Road safety; Life Skills (Decision Making).
slo.keyInquiry: 1. What is statistics? 2. How do we represent data? 3. How do we use statistics in day-to-day life? (Lesson 1 focuses on question 1 and opens questions 2 and 3 on the DQB.)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 gave the claim, the evidence and the three sources of data and started the DQB and the first model. This lesson gives the class the vocabulary and the plan that Lesson 3 needs, when learners start counting the road with tally marks and frequency tables. It addresses KICD key inquiry question 1 (What is statistics?) and opens questions 2 and 3.
slo.safetyNotes: No learner goes onto Thika Road in this lesson. All work is in the classroom, using only the stated claim and the near-miss log. When the real survey is done later, it must be done with Mwalimu Wanjiru and parent or guardian volunteers on a safe footpath, never on the carriageway, and learners must never cross at undesignated spots to count. Treat pedestrian and near-miss stories sensitively, as some learners or relatives may have been involved in road accidents.

LESSONS.overview: Mwalimu Wanjiru recaps the officer's claim, Mzee Otieno's remark and the three sources of data. Learners write in their own words what they think data and statistics mean. In the Observe phase groups sort cards taken from the Thika Road story (the 8,000 m length, the 21 crossing points, the 12 near-misses, the average of about 400 m, the officer's statement, Mzee Otieno's remark, what a learner saw at the gate) into facts or figures (data) and opinions or conclusions, and name the source of each figure. In the Explain phase pairs build a shared definition of data and statistics from their own words, and link statistics to decisions in day-to-day life. The class then clusters the sticky notes on the Driving Question Board, gives each cluster a heading and stars three questions to investigate first. Finally learners add a plan to their first model: the starred questions, the source they will use for each, and a revised sentence about the officer's average. Pacing for a 40-minute period: Predict 4 min, Observe 12 min, Explain 10 min, Driving Question Board 7 min, Model Building 7 min.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the plan from Lesson 1 in a 2-3 minute recap: the officer's claim, Mzee Otieno's remark and the three sources of data (survey, observation, records), using their source tables. Then, individually on a slip, they write: 'In my own words, data are ... and statistics is ... One Thika Road example is ...' They keep the slip to compare with the class definition later.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Last lesson we named three sources of data. Today we decide what data actually are.' Ask two learners to recall one source each, with a Thika Road example. Give 2 minutes of silent writing. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before anyone reads. Cold-call 2 learners to read their slips without comment. Do not give a definition yet.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain: writing a definition before any teaching exposes learners' own ideas (for example that data means only numbers, or only a graph) and gives them something to compare with later.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: slips that mention facts, figures, counting or measuring; slips that mix up data with the conclusion drawn from it; slips that already link statistics to deciding something. Note learners who leave the slip blank for support in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups of four receive eight cards from the Thika Road story: 'the stretch is 8,000 m long', 'there are 21 designated crossing points', 'the drivers logged 12 near-misses', 'the average gap is about 400 m', 'the road is well served' (the officer's statement), 'most near-misses happen in one stretch' (Mzee Otieno's remark), 'I saw learners dashing across at the gate this morning', and 'the road feels dangerous to me'. Groups sort each card into 'a fact or figure that was measured, counted or recorded (data)' or 'an opinion or a conclusion', and for each data card name the source (survey, observation or records). They record one card they could not decide on and say why. A group spokesperson reports one decision.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'You are sorting evidence from opinion.' Circulate and ask: 'Who measured this? Who wrote it down? Could someone check it?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. Prompt groups that stall: 'Is the officer's statement a figure, or a conclusion drawn from a figure?' (The 400 m is a figure; 'well served' is a conclusion.) Accept that 'what I saw at the gate' becomes data once it is recorded carefully, for example in a tally. Cold-call 3 groups, one card each. Do not give counts or gap lengths, and do not calculate.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Card sort (classification routine). Separating figures from conclusions shows that data are what we measure, count or record, and that a conclusion has to be tested against data. This builds the idea that the officer's claim can be checked.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) the 8,000 m, 21 crossing points, 12 near-misses and 400 m cards sorted as data; (2) 'well served' and 'the road feels dangerous' sorted as conclusions or opinions; (3) a correct source named for each data card (for example near-miss log = records; counting and measuring = observation); (4) a reasoned comment on an undecided card. Use a checklist with these four indicators. Groups with several errors are asked to say how each piece of information was obtained (asked, watched or read).

framework.learnerExperience: Pairs build a working meaning of data and statistics. Step 1: each pair rewrites its Predict slip using the card sort, with Thika Road examples (the 8,000 m length, 21 crossing points, 12 near-misses). Step 2: the class agrees a shared definition on the board: Data are facts, figures or observations collected about something; statistics is the collecting, organising, representing and interpreting of data to make decisions. Learners also state that the officer's 400 m is itself a figure that came from data (the length of the road and the number of crossing points), and give one day-to-day use of statistics (for example a county deciding where to build a footbridge, a farmer in Kericho deciding when to pick tea, or a matatu sacco choosing routes).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'In your own words, what are data? Compare with your slip.' Cold-call 4 pairs, e.g. 'Kiprop and partner, give us your definition of data.' Use their words to build the class definition and do not simply dictate it. Press for the use of 'data' as plural: 'These data show...' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Ask: 'If we only knew the officer's figure, what else would we need to know?' Name the sub-strand key idea: 'To decide whether the road is well served we must collect data, organise it, represent it and interpret it.' Do not teach calculation of mean, median or mode; if asked, say 'We will test this in Lesson 5.' Language support: write each key word on the board with an example and, where it helps, a Kiswahili term beside it (for example takwimu for statistics, wastani for average, jedwali la masafa for frequency table). Let learners talk in Kiswahili or their home language first, then say it in English. Teachers should confirm the terms they use.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured pair talk, then whole-class definition building from learners' own words (consensus discourse). Learners connect the abstract terms data and statistics to a concrete decision about their own road.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) definitions that include collecting facts or figures and using them to answer a question or make a decision; (2) correct use of 'data' as plural by at least half of the pairs; (3) recognition that the officer's average is itself data-based; (4) a sensible day-to-day example. Use a thumbs up, sideways, down check on 'I can explain what data are and name three sources'. Pairs who show sideways or down get a follow-up question on a Thika Road example.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups take the sticky notes posted in Lesson 1 and cluster similar notes, giving each cluster a heading (for example 'Spacing of crossing points', 'Where near-misses happen', 'Showing data in a picture', 'Can one number describe a road?'). They add any new question that today's work raised. Notes stay under the three KICD key inquiry columns, or in 'Not sure yet'. The class then chooses 3 questions to investigate first and marks them with a star.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Which questions can data help us answer?' Invite 3 groups to read their cluster headings. Cold-call 2 learners to say which KICD column a cluster fits and why. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds when asking where a question belongs. Point out that many notes about 'how to show it in a picture' belong under 'How do we represent data?'. Guide the class to star questions about counting the gaps, spacing and where near-misses happen. Use the starred questions to connect forward: counting and tallying (Lesson 3), which average to trust (Lesson 5) and graphs (Lessons 10 and 12). Do not promise answers yet.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with question clustering. Clustering and starring make the class agenda visible, and tie learners' own curiosity to the sub-strand outcomes.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) correct placement of notes under the three KICD questions; (2) clusters that have a meaningful heading; (3) starred questions that data could answer; (4) learners who give a reason for a placement. Record the number of notes per column and keep a photograph of the board.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners take out the initial model from Lesson 1 and extend it with a plan: they list the three starred questions and, beside each, the data source they would use (survey, observation or records) and one safety or accuracy point. Then they rewrite the sentence 'The officer's average of 400 m is ...' (true / false / true but not enough, with a reason), and compare it with what they wrote in Lesson 1. Pairs swap books and say whether the plan is realistic and safe. As a take-home task, learners ask one adult (a parent, guardian or matatu driver, if safe and possible) where on Thika Road people cross away from the crossings, and record the answer as a first small survey.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Add to your model a plan for how we will find out.' Circulate and ask: 'Which source for this question? How will you keep safe? How will you keep the record honest?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to read one planned question and source. Remind learners that the 400 m average is true as arithmetic and that the plan is to test whether it is complete. Close by saying: 'Next lesson we start counting the road using tally marks. Think about how we will keep accurate records.' Collect the models for later comparison.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision. Adding a plan to the first model shows learners how their thinking is moving from opinion towards evidence, and the safety and accuracy points keep Integrity visible.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) a source that fits each starred question; (2) a safety or accuracy point for each; (3) a revised 'true but not enough' sentence with a reason; (4) a model that has changed since Lesson 1. Exit question: 'Which source will you use to count the pedestrians who cross away from the zebra crossings, and why?'

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, review the Predict slips and the card sorts. Did learners use 'data' as a plural? Which cards caused disagreement (the officer's statement or 'what I saw at the gate'), and did the discussion stay respectful of Ms Abdi, whose figure is true but possibly incomplete? Were the starred questions testable with data? Which learners were quiet and need a role in Lesson 3 (for example Achieng's tally group)? Are the parent or guardian volunteers for the data collection confirmed? Adjust the Lesson 3 groupings and the tally sheet design in light of this evidence.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We sorted facts and figures from the Thika Road story (the 8,000 m length, 21 crossing points, 12 near-misses and the average of about 400 m) from conclusions and opinions (the road is well served; the road feels dangerous), and we named the source of each figure.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that data are facts, figures or observations collected about something, and that statistics is collecting, organising, representing and interpreting data to make decisions. We learned that a conclusion has to be tested against data, and that statistics helps people make decisions in day-to-day life.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can explain that the officer's 400 m is itself a figure that came from data, but her conclusion that the road is well served is something we can test. We have chosen three questions to investigate first and a source and a safe way to answer each one, and we will keep adding to the Driving Question Board and our model.

LESSONS.title: Counting the Road: Tally Marks and the Frequency Table of the Gaps
LESSONS.aresKeywords: tally, frequency, frequency distribution table, ungrouped data, gap, undesignated crossing, total frequency, data

slo.purpose: Learners collect data with tally marks and organise the 20 ungrouped gap lengths on the 8,000 m stretch of Thika Road into a frequency distribution table, so that the gaps can be examined beyond the officer's single average of 400 m.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (a) collect data from real-life sources using tally marks in bundles of five; (b) draw a frequency distribution table for ungrouped data (gap lengths); (c) check that total frequency equals the number of observations (20 gaps, one fewer than the 21 crossing points); (d) read the table to say which gap length is most common and how many gaps are 300 m or shorter.
slo.skills: Recording with tallies in bundles of five; sorting and ordering raw data; building frequency tables with columns for value, tally and frequency; checking totals; reading a frequency table to spot unusual values. NGSS-style practices embedded: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations, Analyzing and Interpreting Data, Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking, Constructing Explanations.
slo.attitudes: Integrity: the learner collects and records data accurately. Unity: the learner works in groups to tally and tabulate. Core competencies: Critical thinking and problem solving; Communication and collaboration. PCI: Road safety; Life Skills (Decision Making).
slo.keyInquiry: What is statistics? How do we represent data? How do we use statistics in day-to-day life? (Focus today: How do we represent data?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 and Lesson 2 raised the officer's claim (about 400 m average; 8,000 m; 21 crossing points), the near-miss log and the plan to measure gaps and count pedestrians. This lesson turns the plan for the gaps into organised evidence: one ungrouped frequency table for the 20 gaps. Lesson 4 does the same for the pedestrian counts, and Lesson 5 uses both tables to calculate averages. No averages are calculated in this lesson, only organised.
slo.safetyNotes: All data is collected from records and from the classroom tally sheets; no learner goes onto Thika Road during the lesson. For any real field counting, use a safe spot away from the carriageway with a teacher or adult, never step on the road, and wear bright clothing. Handle tape measures and trundle wheels carefully.

LESSONS.overview: Ruaraka Hills Secondary School is on Thika Road, Nairobi. Mwalimu Wanjiru reminds learners of the plan: to test Ms Halima Abdi's claim, the class must measure the 20 gaps between the 21 designated crossing points in metres and count pedestrians crossing at undesignated spots in each gap during the Tuesday 6:30-7:30 am count. Learners predict what a table of the 20 gap lengths will show. First they practise tallying with a quick classroom mini-survey of lunch choices (ugali with sukuma wiki, githeri, rice and beans, or mandazi), with Achieng recording tallies in bundles of five. Then groups work from the raw gap list G1 200 m, G2 150 m, G3 250 m, and so on to G20 200 m, and build the ungrouped frequency table (100:3, 150:2, 200:4, 250:3, 300:2, 600:1, 700:1, 800:1, 1000:1, 1050:1, 1100:1; total 20). They check that the total frequency is 20 and that gap length x frequency adds up to the 8,000 m of the road. In the Explain phase they read the table: most gaps are short but a handful are very long. The DQB and the class model are updated, and the pedestrian counts are left for Lesson 4. Pacing for a 40-minute period: Predict 4 min, Observe 15 min, Explain 10 min, Driving Question Board 4 min, Model Building 7 min.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the plan from Lessons 1 and 2. Mwalimu Wanjiru shows the raw list of the 20 gap lengths in order along the road (G1 to G20) on the board, unsorted and unorganised. Individually (2 minutes) they write a prediction in their books: 'If I organise these 20 gaps into a table, what will I see? Will most gaps be near 400 m, or not?' They also predict: 'Which gap lengths will appear most often?' Then they share with a partner and one group sketches the table they expect.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Last lesson we planned to measure gaps and count pedestrians. Here is what the survey team recorded. Before we organise it, what do you expect to find? Write one prediction and one reason.' Display the raw list without commentary. Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking: 'Does a list in this order make it easy to say which gaps are common?' Cold-call 4 learners (one from each corner of the room) to read their predictions without evaluating them. Ask: 'Who predicted that most gaps would be near 400 m? Raise your hand.' Count and record on the board. Say: 'Keep your prediction; we will test it with a table.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-then-test with a Think-Pair-Share: Writing a prediction first commits learners to an idea about the officer's average, so the later table gives them something to confirm or challenge. It builds understanding because they feel the need for an organising tool when the raw list looks messy.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable: (1) Every learner has a written prediction with a reason before discussion. (2) At least 4 distinct predictions are shared. (3) Note the number of learners who expect most gaps near 400 m (this is revisited in the Explain phase). (4) Listen for learners who say a list is 'hard to read' or 'too messy', showing readiness for tallies.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A (6 minutes): Tally practice. Groups of 5 conduct a mini-survey of their own: 'Which food did you eat for lunch yesterday: ugali with sukuma wiki, githeri, rice and beans, or mandazi?' Achieng's role in each group records tally marks in bundles of five (||||/). Groups then write the frequency for each food. Part B (9 minutes): Groups work with the Thika Road tally sheets. Using the raw list of 20 gap lengths (G1 200 m, G2 150, G3 250, G4 100, G5 300, G6 200, G7 100, G8 250, G9 700, G10 1000, G11 1100, G12 800, G13 1050, G14 600, G15 200, G16 150, G17 100, G18 250, G19 300, G20 200), they make a table with columns: Gap length (m) | Tally | Frequency. They list each different value in order from smallest to largest, tick off each of the 20 gaps once as they tally, and total the frequency column. Kiprop checks the table is ordered and Njeri checks the frequency total is 20.
framework.teacherMoves: Circulate with a checklist. Say: 'Tally in fives: four vertical strokes and a diagonal line across. Why do we bundle in fives?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Use these prompts: 'Show me how you make sure no gap is counted twice.' (for example, strike through each value on the raw list as you tally). 'What should the frequency column add up to? Why?' (20, one for each gap). For the 21 designated crossing points, ask: 'Why are there 20 gaps and not 21?' (Between 21 points there are 20 spaces.) If a group's total is not 20, say: 'Your frequencies add up to 19. Which gap might you have missed? Go back to the list and check G1 to G20 in order.' Do not give the answer. Once groups finish the gap table, pause the room and ask: 'If you multiply each gap length by its frequency and add, what total do you expect, and why?' (8,000 m, the length of the road.) The full calculation of the mean is in Lesson 5; here only the total is checked.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data organising routine (raw list to tally to frequency table) with a Check-the-Total protocol: moving from messy data to a structured table shows how organisation reveals patterns. The total check (20 gaps, 8,000 m) models accuracy and Integrity, so groups trust their table before drawing conclusions.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) tally marks are grouped in fives and counted correctly; (2) values are listed in ascending order with no repeats; (3) the gap table matches 100:3, 150:2, 200:4, 250:3, 300:2, 600:1, 700:1, 800:1, 1000:1, 1050:1, 1100:1 with total frequency 20; (4) groups verify that gap length x frequency adds to 8,000 m. Use a checklist to record groups who need support (for example missed values or wrong order).

framework.learnerExperience: Groups compare their gap frequency tables with a neighbouring group, then with the class master table on the board. They look at the gap table and answer in writing: (1) Which gap length appears most often? (200 m, 4 times.) (2) How many gaps are 300 m or shorter? (14 of the 20.) (3) How many gaps are longer than 300 m, and how long are they? (6 gaps, all from 600 m to 1,100 m.) Learners then discuss: 'Does the table support the officer's statement that the road is well served? What does the table show that one number, 400 m, hides?' They write one claim-evidence-reasoning statement using the frequency column as evidence.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at your table, not at the raw list. What can you see in 30 seconds that you could not see in the list?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 5 learners with different observations. Press for evidence: 'Which row of the table tells you that?' Then ask: 'Ms Halima Abdi said the average gap is about 400 m. Look at your frequency column: how many gaps are actually close to 400 m?' (None are exactly 400 m; 14 are 300 m or shorter and 6 are 600 m or more.) Say: 'The officer's claim is true but incomplete. The 400 m is correct arithmetic (8,000 m / 20 gaps) but the table shows two groups of gaps.' Hold back Lesson 5 content: if a learner offers 'mean, median, mode', say: 'Good words. We calculate them in Lesson 5; today we ask what the table shows us.' Collect 3 CER statements aloud.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with a Notice-and-Wonder routine: learners notice features of the table (clusters, gaps in values, repeated values, unusual values) and then connect them to the phenomenon. The evidence comes directly from their own organised data, which makes the officer's claim testable.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable: (1) learners cite frequencies as evidence (for example, 'the 200 m gap appears 4 times' or '14 gaps are 300 m or shorter'); (2) CER statements mention both the correct arithmetic of the 400 m and the pattern in the table; (3) learners distinguish the six long gaps from the rest; (4) listen for the misconceptions 'the table proves the road is dangerous everywhere' or 'the officer is wrong'; correct with 'true but incomplete'. Exit prompt on a slip: 'Write one thing the frequency table shows that a single average does not.'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the DQB with the three KICD key inquiry questions. Each group adds one sticky-note piece of evidence under 'How do we represent data?' (for example, 'Tally marks and a frequency table organise the 20 gaps') and one new question, such as 'Which gap length is typical?', 'How can we find the middle value?' or 'Where on the road are the long gaps?' They sort the notes into 'Can answer soon' and 'Need more tools'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at our Driving Question. What did today's table add?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 2 groups to read one sticky note each and say which key inquiry question it connects to. Mark any question about pedestrian counts for Lesson 4 and any question about averages for Lesson 5. Model a good question: 'A strong question is one the data could help us answer.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with question clustering: sorting questions makes the learning pathway visible and shows learners that today's table raises questions that later tools will answer.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable: (1) each group posts at least one evidence note and one new question; (2) questions refer to the data (gaps, pedestrians, near-misses) rather than generic topics; (3) learners link notes to the right key inquiry question.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise their initial model from Lesson 1. On the line for the 8,000 m of Thika Road they add a mini frequency table of the gap lengths and mark the six long gaps (600 m to 1,100 m). They write a short note: 'Our table shows that the officer's 400 m is correct but many gaps are short and a few are very long.' They add one thing they still cannot explain, and one question about the pedestrians: 'How many people cross away from the zebra crossings in each gap?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Revise your model. What new piece of evidence goes into it today, and what question does your model still not answer?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Circulate and ask 3 learners: 'Where in your model would a reader see that the road is not evenly served?' Ask two volunteers to share. Hand-off: 'Next lesson we organise the second table, the number of pedestrians crossing in each gap, and see whether the long gaps and the pedestrian counts go together. Keep your tally sheets safe.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: adding the table to the evolving model shows how evidence changes the explanation, and the unanswered pedestrian question gives the next lesson its purpose.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable: (1) revised models include the frequency table or its key rows; (2) the model distinguishes short gaps from the six long ones; (3) learners state a remaining question. Record who can say, in their own words, why a tally and frequency table help in testing the officer's claim.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: Did every group's gap table total 20 and give 8,000 m when gap length is multiplied by frequency? Which groups needed help with ordering values or missed a gap? Which learners confused frequency (how many gaps) with the gap value (metres)? Did learners say 'the officer is wrong', and how did I reframe it as 'true but incomplete'? What would I change about the tally practice to give quieter learners more speaking time? Remember this is a one-morning sample (Tuesday, 6:30-7:30 am) and may need repeating.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We tallied the 20 gaps between the 21 designated crossing points on the 8,000 m stretch of Thika Road. Our frequency table showed that gap lengths of 100 m to 300 m are common (14 of the 20 gaps), while six gaps are between 600 m and 1,100 m. We checked that the frequencies add up to 20 and that gap length x frequency adds up to 8,000 m.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Tally marks (in bundles of five) help us collect data, and a frequency distribution table for ungrouped data organises it so that we can check the total (20 gaps) and see which values are common or unusual.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The officer's 400 m average is true but incomplete. Our frequency table shows that most gaps are short while a few are very long, which suggests that a single number hides where pedestrians may be at risk. We still need to organise the pedestrian counts and then use averages to describe the data fairly.

LESSONS.title: Pedestrians per Gap: A Second Frequency Table and Where the Large Counts Are
LESSONS.aresKeywords: tally, frequency, frequency distribution table, ungrouped data, gap, undesignated crossing, total frequency, data, pedestrians per gap

slo.purpose: Learners organise the number of pedestrians who cross at undesignated spots in each of the 20 gaps into an ungrouped frequency table, check its totals (20 gaps and 182 pedestrians), and notice that the six large counts match the six long gaps, without calculating any average.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (a) collect data from real-life sources using tally marks (pedestrians per gap); (b) draw a frequency distribution table for ungrouped data; (c) check that the total frequency equals 20 gaps and that pedestrians per gap x frequency adds to 182; (d) read the table to compare the pedestrian counts with the gap lengths.
slo.skills: Recording with tallies in bundles of five; sorting and ordering raw data; building frequency tables with columns for value, tally and frequency; checking totals; reading a frequency table to spot unusual values. NGSS-style practices embedded: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations, Analyzing and Interpreting Data, Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking, Constructing Explanations.
slo.attitudes: Integrity: the learner collects and records data accurately. Unity: the learner works in groups to tally and tabulate. Core competencies: Critical thinking and problem solving; Communication and collaboration. PCI: Road safety; Life Skills (Decision Making).
slo.keyInquiry: What is statistics? How do we represent data? How do we use statistics in day-to-day life? (Focus today: How do we represent data?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 3 organised the 20 gap lengths. This lesson organises the second data set from the same morning count, the pedestrians crossing at undesignated spots in each gap. The two tables together are the input for Lesson 5, where mean, median and mode are calculated. No averages are calculated in this lesson, only organised.
slo.safetyNotes: All data is collected from records and from the classroom tally sheets; no learner goes onto Thika Road during the lesson. For any real field counting, use a safe spot away from the carriageway with a teacher or adult, never step on the road, and wear bright clothing. Handle tape measures and trundle wheels carefully.

LESSONS.overview: Mwalimu Wanjiru recaps the gap table from the last lesson. Learners predict whether pedestrians cross evenly along the road or in some gaps more than others. Groups then build the ungrouped frequency table for pedestrians per gap from the raw tally sheet (G1 3, G2 2, G3 4, G4 1, G5 5, G6 3, G7 2, G8 4, G9 18, G10 26, G11 31, G12 22, G13 28, G14 15, G15 4, G16 2, G17 1, G18 3, G19 5, G20 3), giving 1:2, 2:3, 3:4, 4:3, 5:2, 15:1, 18:1, 22:1, 26:1, 28:1, 31:1 with a total of 20 gaps, and check that pedestrians per gap x frequency adds up to 182. In the Explain phase learners place the pedestrian table beside the gap table and notice that the counts of 15 to 31 match the six long gaps G9 to G14, though no average is calculated. They add questions to the DQB and extend the model with both tables. Pacing for a 40-minute period: Predict 4 min, Observe 14 min, Explain 10 min, Driving Question Board 6 min, Model Building 6 min.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the gap table from Lesson 3 in a 2-3 minute recap (14 gaps of 300 m or shorter, six gaps of 600 m to 1,100 m). Mwalimu Wanjiru explains that the same morning count recorded how many pedestrians crossed away from the zebra crossings in each gap. Individually (2 minutes) learners write a prediction: 'Will the pedestrians be spread evenly over the 20 gaps, or will some gaps have many more than others? Which gaps do you think they will be?' They share with a partner and one group sketches the table they expect.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Last lesson we organised the gap lengths. Here is the second part of the count: pedestrians in each gap. Before we organise it, what do you expect to find? Write one prediction and one reason.' Do not show the raw list yet. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after asking: 'Would you expect the same number of pedestrians in a 100 m gap as in a 1,000 m gap?' Cold-call 4 learners to read their predictions without evaluating them. Record the number of learners who expect an even spread. Say: 'Keep your prediction; we will test it with a table.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-then-test with Think-Pair-Share: writing a prediction first commits learners to an idea about how pedestrians are spread, so the later table gives them something to confirm or challenge.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable: (1) every learner has a written prediction with a reason; (2) note the number who expect an even spread and those who link more pedestrians to longer gaps; (3) listen for learners who say a list is 'hard to read', showing readiness for a table.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups work with the Thika Road tally sheet for pedestrians per gap, using the raw list (G1 3, G2 2, G3 4, G4 1, G5 5, G6 3, G7 2, G8 4, G9 18, G10 26, G11 31, G12 22, G13 28, G14 15, G15 4, G16 2, G17 1, G18 3, G19 5, G20 3). They make a table with columns: Pedestrians in the gap | Tally | Frequency, list each different value from smallest to largest, tick off each of the 20 gaps once as they tally, and total the frequency column. Kiprop checks the table is ordered and Njeri checks that the frequency total is 20. Groups then check the second total: pedestrians per gap x frequency should add up to 182, the number of pedestrians counted on the whole stretch.
framework.teacherMoves: Circulate with a checklist. Ask: 'Show me how you make sure no gap is counted twice.' 'What should the frequency column add up to? Why?' (20, one for each gap, not 182.) Draw out the difference between the two totals: 'Which total counts gaps and which counts people?' If a group's total is not 20, say: 'Which gap might you have missed? Go back to the list and check G1 to G20 in order.' Do not give the answer. When groups finish, pause the room and ask: 'Multiply each value by its frequency and add; what total do you expect?' (182.) WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. The calculation of the mean number of pedestrians per gap is in Lesson 5; here only the totals are checked.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data organising routine (raw list to tally to frequency table) with a Check-the-Total protocol. Two totals (20 gaps, 182 pedestrians) show learners what a frequency counts and what the value counts, and model accuracy and Integrity.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) tally marks grouped in fives and counted correctly; (2) values listed in ascending order with no repeats; (3) the table matches 1:2, 2:3, 3:4, 4:3, 5:2, 15:1, 18:1, 22:1, 26:1, 28:1, 31:1 with total 20 gaps; (4) groups verify that value x frequency adds to 182 pedestrians. Use a checklist to record groups who need support (missed values, wrong order, or confusing 20 with 182).

framework.learnerExperience: Groups put the pedestrian table beside the gap table from Lesson 3. They look at the pedestrian table: the counts of 1 to 5 appear for 14 gaps, but 15, 18, 22, 26, 28 and 31 each appear once. They link the large counts and the long gaps: the six large counts match the six long gaps G9 to G14, though they do not yet compute any average. Learners discuss: 'Does the table support the officer's statement that the road is well served? Which rows of the pedestrian table might Mzee Otieno mean when he says most near-misses are in one stretch?' They write a claim-evidence-reasoning statement using both tables.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at your two tables side by side. What can you see that a single average of 400 m hides?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners with different observations. Press for evidence: 'Which row of which table tells you that?' Ask: 'Mzee Otieno says most near-misses happen in one stretch. Which rows of the pedestrian table might that be?' Say: 'The officer's claim is true but incomplete.' Hold back Lesson 5 content: if a learner offers 'mean, median, mode', say: 'Good words. We calculate them in Lesson 5; today we ask what the tables show us.' Collect 3 CER statements aloud.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with a Notice-and-Wonder routine: learners notice features of two tables (clusters, repeated values, unusually large values) and connect them to the phenomenon. The evidence comes directly from their own organised data.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable: (1) learners cite frequencies as evidence (for example 'the six biggest counts are in the six long gaps'); (2) CER statements mention both the correct arithmetic of the 400 m and the pattern in the tables; (3) learners distinguish the six large counts from the 14 small ones; (4) correct the misconception that 'the table proves the road is dangerous everywhere' or 'the officer is wrong' with 'true but incomplete'. Exit prompt on a slip: 'Write one thing the two tables show that a single average does not.'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the DQB started in Lesson 1, with the three KICD key inquiry questions: What is statistics? How do we represent data? How do we use statistics in day-to-day life? Each group adds sticky-note evidence under 'How do we represent data?' (for example, 'Tally marks and frequency tables organise 20 gaps and 182 pedestrians') and writes at least one new question on a sticky note, such as 'Which gap length is typical?', 'How can we find the middle value?', 'The table has many values; can we group them?' or 'Where on the road do the large pedestrian counts happen?' They place the notes on the board and sort them into 'Can answer soon' and 'Need more tools'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at our Driving Question: How can we use data from our own road to show where pedestrians are really at risk, and why does one average not tell the whole story? What did today's tables add?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups to read one sticky note each and say which key inquiry question it connects to. Say: 'Who can link this note to Lesson 5, where we will calculate mean, median and mode?' Highlight any question about averages and mark it for next lesson. Cluster questions about grouping into classes and tag them for Lesson 7. Model a good question: 'A strong question is one the data could help us answer.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with question clustering: sorting questions makes the learning pathway visible. It builds understanding by showing learners that today's tables raise new questions that later tools (averages, grouping, graphs) will answer.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable: (1) Each group posts at least one evidence note and one new question. (2) Questions refer to the data (gaps, pedestrians, near-misses) rather than generic topics. (3) Learners correctly link notes to the key inquiry questions. (4) Notice whether at least two groups ask about averages or about where the risk is greatest.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise their model from Lesson 1 in their books. On the line for the 8,000 m of Thika Road they add both tables in simple form: the gap table from Lesson 3 and the pedestrian table from today, and they write the data-handling steps as Collect (tally), Organise (frequency table), Check (totals 20 gaps, 8,000 m, 182 pedestrians). They mark the six long gaps (600 m to 1,100 m) beside the six pedestrian counts of 15 to 31. They write a short note: 'Our tables show that the officer's 400 m is correct but many gaps are short and a few are very long, and the large pedestrian counts are in the long gaps.' They add one thing they still cannot explain, for example 'which number best represents the typical gap'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Revise your model. What new piece of evidence goes into it today, and what question does your model still not answer?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Circulate and ask 3 learners: 'Where in your model would a reader see that the road is not evenly served?' Push for specifics: 'Point to the part of your table that shows it.' Ask two volunteers to share their revised models. Close by saying: 'Next lesson we ask which measure, mean, median or mode, tells the truth about these 20 gaps. Keep your tables safe; you will use them.' Remind learners to keep tally sheets and tables in their project folders.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: adding the data-handling process and both tables to the evolving model shows how evidence changes the explanation. Learners see the model becoming more precise and recognise its remaining gaps.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable: (1) revised models include both frequency tables or their key rows; (2) models show the totals 20 gaps, 8,000 m and 182 pedestrians; (3) the model links the six long gaps to the six large counts; (4) learners identify a remaining question (for example, which average to use). Record who can state, in their own words, why a tally and frequency table help in testing the officer's claim.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: Did every group's pedestrian table total 20 gaps and 182 pedestrians? Which learners confused frequency (how many gaps) with the value (how many pedestrians)? Did learners link the six large counts to the six long gaps? How did I reframe 'the officer is wrong' as 'true but incomplete'? Which DQB questions about averages or grouping should open Lesson 5 and Lesson 7? Remember this is a one-morning sample (Tuesday, 6:30-7:30 am) and may need repeating.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We tallied the pedestrians crossing at undesignated spots in each of the 20 gaps on the 8,000 m stretch of Thika Road (182 in total). Our frequency table showed that counts of 1 to 5 occurred in 14 gaps, while six gaps had counts of 15 to 31, matching the six long gaps of 600 m to 1,100 m.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: A frequency distribution table for ungrouped data organises counts so that we can check two totals: the total frequency (20 gaps) and the total of value x frequency (182 pedestrians). We learned to tell what a frequency counts from what the value counts.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The officer's 400 m average is true but incomplete. Our two tables show that most gaps are short with few pedestrians, while a handful of very long gaps carry very large counts, so a single number hides where pedestrians may be at risk. We need mean, median and mode to describe the data fairly.
