LESSONS.title: The Median of Grouped Data: Cumulative Frequency and the Median Class
LESSONS.aresKeywords: grouped data, cumulative frequency, median class, grouped median, estimate, n/2, class width, Thika Road gaps

slo.purpose: Learners estimate the median of the grouped Thika Road gap data using cumulative frequency and the median formula, compare it with the ungrouped median (250 m), and use the comparison to revise the class model of why one average cannot show where pedestrians are at risk.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to determine the median of grouped data (KICD Specific Learning Outcome c). Learners know how to build a cumulative frequency column, locate the median class from n/2, and use the grouped median = L + ((n/2 - cf)/f) x w, where L is the lower boundary of the median class, cf the cumulative frequency before it, f its frequency and w its width. They know that the result is an estimate that differs from the ungrouped median.
slo.skills: Calculating midpoints; completing an f x midpoint column and summing it; building a cumulative frequency column; locating the median class from n/2; substituting into the median formula; comparing estimates with true values; Critical thinking and problem solving (NGSS SEP: Analyzing and interpreting data; Using mathematics and computational thinking).
slo.attitudes: Integrity: learner records and calculates accurately and reports differences between estimates and true values honestly. Unity: learner works in groups, sharing roles (Achieng data, Kiprop calculations, Njeri graphs). Love: learner is considerate of group members as they check each other's working. Life skills (Decision Making): learner sees why decisions about road safety need more than one average.
slo.keyInquiry: KICD key inquiry questions: 1. What is statistics? 2. How do we represent data? 3. How do we use statistics in day-to-day life? This lesson advances Q2 and Q3: How does grouping change the averages we calculate, and can we trust an estimate when making decisions about a road?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 8 estimated the grouped mean (440 m). This lesson estimates the grouped median (311 m) from the same table and compares it with the true median of 250 m. Learners see that both the mean and the median still sit far from the long 600 m to 1,100 m gaps in the long stretch G9-G14. The comparison feeds the class model and prepares for the histograms in Lesson 10.
slo.safetyNotes: This is a classroom calculation lesson. Any data collection or road observation is NOT done in this lesson; use the recorded Thika Road data only. If learners discuss the road, remind them never to cross at undesignated spots, and to cross only at zebra crossings or footbridges. Keep walkways between desks clear while groups move to the board.

LESSONS.overview: Learners recall the grouped mean (440 m) and the true mean (400 m). They predict whether the grouped median will be higher, lower or the same as the true median (250 m), and which class it falls in. They then build the cumulative frequency column (5, 14, 14, 16, 17, 20), find the median class (200 to <400), and use the formula to get 200 + ((10-5)/9) x 200 = 311 m. In the Explain phase they compare 311 m with 250 m and 440 m with 400 m, explain why grouping makes the estimates differ, and connect the averages back to the phenomenon: both the mean and the median, ungrouped or grouped, describe a typical gap of 250 m to 440 m, yet six gaps of 600 m to 1,100 m sit in the long stretch G9-G14 that includes the school gate. The class updates the DQB and revises the model. Pacing for a 40-minute period: Predict 4 min, Observe 14 min, Explain 10 min, Driving Question Board 5 min, Model Building 7 min.

framework.learnerExperience: (4 min) Learners recall from Lesson 8: the grouped mean is an estimate (440 m) of the true mean (400 m). The ordered gap list gave a true median of 250 m (Lesson 6). Individually they write a prediction: 'If we estimate the median from the grouped table, will we get 250 m exactly, a bit higher, or a bit lower? In which class do you think the 10th and 11th gaps fall?' Pairs share with a neighbouring pair and record a group prediction on the prediction chart.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the grouped table (classes 0 to <200, 200 to <400, 400 to <600, 600 to <800, 800 to <1000, 1000 to <1200 with frequencies 5, 9, 0, 2, 1, 3). Say: 'The true median is 250 m. Now we only have this table. What will the median estimate be?' Give 1 minute silent writing, then WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after asking: 'Which class do you think the 10th and 11th gaps fall in?' Cold-call 3 learners to share predictions and reasons without saying whether they are right. Record the 3 most common predictions on the board.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction chart and Think-Pair-Share: writing a prediction before calculating commits learners to an idea, so that any difference between 250 m and the grouped estimate becomes a puzzle to explain.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) at least 80% of learners have a written prediction with a reason; (2) learners who locate the middle gaps in the class 200 to <400 from the frequencies; (3) note how many predict the grouped median will be exactly 250 m. Use the thumbs show (up = same, sideways = close but different, down = very different) and record counts for the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: (14 min) In groups of 4 learners add a cumulative frequency column to the grouped table (5, 14, 14, 16, 17, 20), find n/2 = 10, see that the 10th value lies in the class 200 to <400 (cf before it = 5, f = 9, L = 200, w = 200) and calculate 200 + ((10 - 5)/9) x 200 = 311 m (311.1, to the nearest metre). They record the estimate on a results card and place it beside the ungrouped median of 250 m and the grouped mean of 440 m.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the grouped table and calculators. Ask: 'Why does the cumulative frequency stay 14 in the third row?' and 'Where in the cumulative column do we first reach or pass 10?' Cold-call 3 learners. Write the formula L + ((n/2 - cf)/f) x w on the board and label each symbol with an arrow to the table. Circulate with a checklist. After the calculation, ask 3 groups to report their median class and estimate; WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Close with: 'Place your estimate next to 250 m. What do you notice?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured data table with role rotation: building the cumulative frequency column step by step makes the logic of the formula visible. Placing the grouped and ungrouped results side by side creates the evidence needed for the Explain phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) cumulative frequencies 5, 14, 14, 16, 17, 20; (2) the median class 200 to <400 chosen because n/2 = 10; (3) correct substitution L = 200, cf = 5, f = 9, w = 200 and the answer 311 m with the unit and the word 'estimate'. Common errors to note: using f instead of cumulative frequency for cf, using n = 20 instead of n/2 = 10. Rubric alignment: Meets = accurate table and estimate; Approaches = needs help with one of the steps; Below = partially completes the table.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Groups compare their grouped estimates with the ungrouped results on a comparison chart: mean 400 m vs 440 m (grouped estimate, 40 m higher); median 250 m vs 311 m (grouped estimate, 61 m higher). They answer: (1) Why is the grouped median 311 m while the true median is 250 m? (The formula assumes the 9 gaps in 200 to <400 are spread evenly across the class, but in fact they are bunched at 200 m to 300 m.) (2) Which estimate is closer to the truth, and does it change what we can say about the officer's claim? (3) Both averages, grouped or not, describe a typical gap of 250 m to 440 m, yet the six gaps of 600 m to 1,100 m sit in the long stretch G9-G14 that includes the school gate, where 140 of 182 pedestrians crossed at undesignated spots in the one-morning sample. Can any of the four numbers tell Mzee Otieno where the danger is?
framework.teacherMoves: Ask: 'Our predictions on the board said same, close, or very different. Which was right?' Use the thumbs counts. Pose Question 1 and WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Use talk moves: 'Who can add to what Achieng said?' Cold-call 4 learners and ask them to point to the table when explaining. Ask: 'The officer says 400 m; our grouped mean says 440 m; the median says 250 m or 311 m. Is the officer wrong?' Guide learners to say: 'The officer's claim is true but incomplete.' Ask: 'If a matatu driver like Mzee Otieno asks where the danger is, can any of these four numbers tell him?' Take 3 responses and guide to: grouping gives estimates; none of the averages tells us WHERE the long gaps are.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with a comparison chart: learners make a claim (the grouped estimates are close but not exact), support it with the figures 400 vs 440 and 250 vs 311, and give reasoning about even spread within classes. The second reasoning step connects the mathematics to the phenomenon, which advances the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for: (1) learners state that the grouped median is an ESTIMATE; (2) learners explain the difference using the assumption of even spread within a class; (3) learners say the officer's claim is true but incomplete, not wrong; (4) learners link to the long stretch G9-G14 and the 140 of 182 pedestrians. Check with an exit prompt on mini-whiteboards: 'Write one reason the grouped median (311 m) is not 250 m.' Scan for 'spread evenly' or 'we lost the real values'.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Learners return to the class DQB started in Lesson 1. Individually, they write on sticky notes: one thing they now understand (for example 'How to find the estimated mean from midpoints') and one new question (for example 'Can a graph show us where the long gaps are?', 'Why is the grouped median 311 m and not 250 m?', 'Would smaller classes make the estimate closer?'). They place the notes under the three KICD key inquiry questions (What is statistics? How do we represent data? How do we use statistics in day-to-day life?) and mark any earlier questions they can now answer, such as 'How can the mean be correct but the road still dangerous?' (partly answered: the mean is pulled up by a few very long gaps).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Let us look at our board. Which of our earlier questions can we move to Answered or Partly answered?' Give WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners to place notes and justify them. Ask Njeri's group: 'Your question about graphs - which lesson might help?' (preview Lesson 10: histograms). Group similar questions with learners' help. Highlight a question about class width and flag it as a good question for Lessons 10 and 13. Close: 'The grouped mean and median are estimates, but they still do not tell Mzee Otieno where the danger is. What do we need next?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a public record of growing understanding: learners see their questions move from unanswered to partly answered, which makes progress visible and keeps the investigation anchored in the phenomenon. Sorting under the three KICD key inquiry questions links the work to curriculum goals.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that every learner has contributed at least one note; that at least two new questions refer to graphs or to showing WHERE the long gaps are; and that learners correctly place calculation notes under 'How do we represent data?' or 'How do we use statistics in day-to-day life?'. Note learners whose questions repeat Lesson 1 questions without any new content, and prompt them with 'What did the table show that you could not see before?'.

framework.learnerExperience: (15 min) Groups revise their class model (a poster or chart begun in Lesson 1) of why the officer's average does not show where pedestrians are at risk. They add a new section titled 'What grouped averages tell us', containing: the grouped table; the estimated mean 440 m; the grouped median 311 m; the ungrouped mean 400 m and median 250 m; and a short statement, for example: 'Mean (400 m) and median (250 m) describe a typical gap on this 8,000 m stretch of Thika Road in our 20-gap sample. Grouping gives estimates (440 m and 311 m) that are close but not exact. None of these averages shows that six gaps of 600 m to 1,100 m are in one stretch.' Groups then add a 'What we still need' arrow pointing to graphs (Lesson 10: histograms; Lesson 12: frequency polygons) and a note that this is a one-morning sample and should be repeated. Each group shares its model addition in a gallery walk.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Add to your model what today's numbers show and what they still cannot show.' Prompt: 'Use the words estimate, midpoint and cumulative frequency in your model.' Circulate and ask: 'Does your model say the officer is wrong? How could you word it so it is fair to Ms Halima Abdi?' Remind groups that the claim is true but incomplete. Give WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after asking: 'If a learner from Mombasa Road gave you only a grouped table, what could you still work out?' Run the gallery walk: each group leaves one person at the poster while others visit; cold-call 3 visitors to report one idea they borrowed. Finish by asking 2 learners to complete the sentence 'Averages alone cannot show risk because ...'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with gallery walk: adding today's evidence to the existing model shows learners that scientific and mathematical models grow as evidence grows. Writing what the model still cannot explain creates a purposeful need for histograms and polygons in the next lessons, linking directly to the driving question about showing where pedestrians are really at risk.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) the model includes the grouped mean 440 m and grouped median 311 m labelled as estimates; (2) it compares them with 400 m and 250 m; (3) it states a limit: averages do not show where the long gaps are; (4) the wording is respectful: true but incomplete; (5) a next step (graphs) is named. Rubric check: Meets = accurate figures with an explanation; Exceeds = also explains why grouping causes the difference; Approaches = figures with minimal explanation; Below = figures copied without explanation.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson ask yourself: Which groups struggled with n/2 and cumulative frequency in the median formula, and what extra practice (for example a small table of 10 matatu fares from Kisumu to Kakamega) is needed? Could learners explain WHY the grouped median (311 m) differs from 250 m, or only that it does? Did anyone call the grouped answer 'wrong'? Did learners link the averages back to the long stretch G9-G14 and the school gate? Which DQB questions should shape Lesson 10?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We built cumulative frequencies (5, 14, 14, 16, 17, 20) for the grouped Thika Road gap table for the 20-gap sample, found the median class (200 to <400) and a grouped median of 311 m, and compared it with the ungrouped median (250 m). We also compared the grouped mean (440 m) with the ungrouped mean (400 m).
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The median of grouped data is found with cumulative frequency and the formula L + ((n/2 - cf)/f) x w. Grouping loses the exact values, so grouped results are estimates that differ from ungrouped results.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The grouped median (311 m) differs from 250 m because the formula assumes the values are spread evenly in a class. Ms Halima Abdi's 400 m mean is true but incomplete: none of these averages shows that six gaps of 600 m to 1,100 m sit in one 5,250 m stretch near the school gate, so we need graphs of how the gaps are spread, together with the ordered gap list, to show where pedestrians are at risk.

LESSONS.title: Histograms with Equal Class Widths: Seeing the Shape of the Gaps
LESSONS.aresKeywords: histogram, equal class width, continuous axis, bars touch, frequency, gap, Thika Road, long stretch, pedestrians

slo.purpose: Learners draw a histogram of the 20 Thika Road gaps with equal class widths from the grouped table, and read its shape to see that the gaps bunch at the short end while a few long gaps stand apart, which the officer's mean of 400 m does not show.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (d) represent data using histograms (KICD sub-strand outcome d); (e) interpret data from a histogram (outcome e). Learners draw a histogram for equal-width classes (width 200 m) for the 20 gaps on the 8,000 m Thika Road stretch, frequencies 5, 9, 0, 2, 1, 3. Bars touch, the horizontal axis is continuous, and the empty class 400 to <600 is shown as a gap with no bar.
slo.skills: Calculating frequency density; choosing and labelling scales on both axes; drawing bars that touch with correct boundaries; reading the shape of a histogram; explaining why the tallest bar must be judged by frequency density, not frequency, when widths are unequal; using and interpreting graphs as models (NGSS SEP: Developing and Using Models; Analyzing and Interpreting Data; Constructing Explanations).
slo.attitudes: Core competencies: Critical thinking and problem solving (the learner uses the histograms to examine data and make conclusions); Communication and collaboration. Values: Integrity (the learner records and plots data accurately); Unity (the learner works in groups to draw histograms). PCIs: Life Skills (Decision Making); Road safety. Learners are respectful of the officer, whose mean is true but incomplete.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we represent data? (Also tracked: What is statistics? How do we use statistics in day-to-day life?) Lesson question: What does a histogram of the 20 Thika Road gaps show that the mean of 400 m does not, and why must we use frequency density when class widths are unequal?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 7 to 9 gave a grouped table and showed that grouping changes the estimates. Lesson 10 turns the table into a picture for the first time. The class can SEE the cluster of short gaps and the separate long gaps of 600 m to 1,100 m. Lesson 11 then merges classes to make unequal widths and introduces frequency density, and Lessons 12 and 13 draw frequency polygons and compare Thika Road with Mombasa Road.
slo.safetyNotes: The lesson is classroom-based, so no learners go onto the road. If the class revisits the road to check any measurement, this must be done only with Mwalimu Wanjiru and other adults, on the school side of the road, using the designated crossing. Learners must not run across Thika Road to measure anything. Pencils and rulers are used sensibly. Graph paper and charts are shared fairly.

LESSONS.overview: Mwalimu Wanjiru reminds the class of the officer's claim: the average gap between the 21 designated crossing points on the 8,000 m stretch of Thika Road is about 400 m. Ms Halima Abdi's arithmetic is correct, yet Mzee Otieno's matatu near-miss log has 9 of 12 near-misses in one stretch. Learners first predict what a picture of the 20 gaps will look like. They then draw a histogram from the equal-width table (frequencies 5, 9, 0, 2, 1, 3) on graph paper and notice the empty 400 to <600 position and the lonely bars to the right. In the Explain phase they read the histogram: where 400 m falls, where the tall bars are, and what the histogram can and cannot say about WHERE on the road the long gaps are. The class updates the DQB and revises the model. Pacing for a 40-minute period: Predict 4 min, Observe 17 min, Explain 10 min, Driving Question Board 4 min, Model Building 5 min.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the officer's claim and Mzee Otieno's remark. Each learner sketches, in their exercise book, what they think a bar graph of the 20 Thika Road gaps will look like (short, medium and long gaps on the horizontal axis) and writes one sentence: 'I think the picture will show...' They compare with a partner.
framework.teacherMoves: Display on the board: 'Officer: the average gap is about 400 m, so the road is well served. Mzee Otieno: most near-misses are in one stretch.' Ask: "If I drew all 20 gaps as a picture, where would you expect the tall bars? Sketch it silently for 2 minutes." Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking the question before any learner speaks. Circulate and select 3 contrasting sketches. Cold-call 3 learners to describe their sketch without saying whether it is right. Tally on the board how many learners sketched a single hump near 400 m.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (prediction stage) with Public Sketch Comparison: committing to a picture before drawing exposes the common idea that 'average = typical' and gives learners something to test against the real histogram.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: whether sketches place a single hump near 400 m (the mean misconception) or show short gaps plus a tail. Use the tally later to compare with the real histogram.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4 (roles: Achieng-type recorder of tallies, Kiprop-type table and calculation checker, Njeri-type grapher, one reader/checker), learners use graph paper. From the grouped table (0 to <200: 5; 200 to <400: 9; 400 to <600: 0; 600 to <800: 2; 800 to <1000: 1; 1000 to <1200: 3) they draw a histogram with the horizontal axis as gap length in metres (continuous, labelled 0, 200, 400... 1200), vertical axis frequency, bars touching, and a gap with no bar for 400 to <600 (frequency 0). They label both axes and give the graph a title. For learners with low vision or limited fine-motor control, give large-grid paper or a pre-drawn axis, let them lay card strips as bars, and let them describe the histogram aloud instead of shading it.
framework.teacherMoves: Model the first bar on the board: "The first class is 0 to <200, so the bar goes from 0 to 200 on the axis and its height is 5." Say: "Bars touch because the gap length is continuous. Why is there no break between 200 and 400?" Allow WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Circulate and check scales and that the empty class is shown with no bar. Provide extra support cards for learners needing scaffolding (for example pre-labelled axes). Ask: "What does the height of a bar tell us when all the bars have the same width?" Cold-call 2 groups.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data representation and modelling: translating a table into a graph shows how the same numbers produce a shape. Building the bars one by one, with equal widths, lets learners see a histogram as a picture of the frequency column.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) bars touch and have correct boundaries on the continuous axis; (2) the 400 to <600 position is shown with zero height; (3) heights 5, 9, 0, 2, 1, 3; (4) axes labelled 'Gap length (m)' and 'Frequency'. Use a checklist while circulating; note groups who leave spaces between bars or use class labels instead of a number scale.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners use the equal-width histogram to explain the phenomenon. In groups they answer: (1) Where are the tall bars and where are the lonely bars? (2) The officer's mean is 400 m. Where is 400 m on your histogram? Is that where most of the gaps are? (The 400 to <600 position has no bar.) (3) Fourteen of the 20 gaps are 300 m or shorter and six gaps are 600 m to 1,100 m. Which list tells us WHERE on the road those six gaps are? (The ordered gap list G1 to G20: G9 to G14, the long stretch from the 1,550 m mark to the 6,800 m mark, 5,250 m in all, including the school gate at the 4,000 m mark.) They write a 2-sentence explanation: 'The histogram shows... The mean hides this because...'
framework.teacherMoves: Ask: "Look at your histogram. Where is the tall bar, and what does it tell you about most gaps on Thika Road?" WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 learners. Press for evidence: "Which bar shows the gaps of 1,000 m, 1,050 m and 1,100 m?" Then: "The officer's mean is 400 m. Where is 400 m on your histogram? Is it where most of the gaps are?" Say: "Ms Halima Abdi is not wrong; her mean is correct but incomplete. What does the picture add?" Make one distinction explicit: a histogram shows HOW MANY gaps are short or long, not WHERE along the road they are. If a learner points at a bar and says 'this part of the road', ask: 'The bar tells us how many gaps are that long. Which list tells us where they are?' Do not re-teach mean or median (done in Lessons 5, 6, 8 and 9).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with Talk Moves: learners make a claim about what the picture shows, support it with bars from the histogram, and explain why a mean cannot show this. Revoicing and 'add on' talk moves build a shared explanation that connects the graph to the phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for: (1) learners reading the shape correctly (a cluster of short gaps and a separate group of long gaps to the right); (2) learners noticing that few or no gaps are near the mean of 400 m; (3) learners linking the long gaps to the long stretch G9-G14 by using the ordered gap list, not the histogram. Collect the explanations and sort into: describes shape only / links to the mean / links to the long stretch.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class DQB. They add sticky notes: new answers or evidence for the key inquiry questions and new questions arising, such as 'What if two bars were merged into one wide class?', 'Can we show the gap pattern as a line graph?' or 'Which crossing points should be added first?' They mark that 'How do we represent data?' now has the evidence 'histogram with equal class widths'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Take 1 minute silently to write one thing the histogram taught you and one new question. Then place your note on the DQB." WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before inviting the first learner. Cold-call 2 learners to read a note and say which key inquiry question it connects to. Group similar questions and point out that Lesson 11 will deal with classes of different widths.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a public record of learning: sorting questions into answered, partly answered and open shows learners how today's evidence moves the class understanding forward.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that notes are specific (for example mention the empty class or the tall bar) rather than generic. Count how many learners connect a note to one of the 3 KICD key inquiry questions.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class model of the phenomenon (a poster or diagram on a chart). They add a sketch of the histogram and annotate: 'Most gaps are short (14 of 20 are 300 m or shorter). A few very long gaps (600 m to 1,100 m) sit to the right and pull the mean up to 400 m. The histogram shows how many gaps are long; the ordered gap list shows they are in the long stretch G9-G14, 5,250 m, with the school gate.'
framework.teacherMoves: Ask: "What can we now add to our model that we could not show in Lesson 9?" WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to propose one addition each and ask the class to agree or add on. Prompt: "What would you say to Ms Halima Abdi and Mzee Otieno using this graph?" Remind learners that this is a one-morning sample (Tuesday, 6:30-7:30 am) and should be repeated. Hand-off: "Next lesson we merge classes of different widths and meet frequency density."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision: adding the histogram to the model makes the graph a tool for explanation, not just a drawing.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: the revised model (1) names the shape (short gaps cluster plus long gaps to the right), (2) states that the mean of 400 m is true but incomplete, and (3) mentions the long stretch G9-G14 and the 20-gap sample from Thika Road. Use a 3-point check (missing, partial, complete) on each group's poster.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: Did learners see the empty 400 to <600 position and realise that few gaps are near the mean of 400 m? Which groups left spaces between bars or used a non-uniform scale? Which learners can read the histogram but cannot yet link it to the ordered gap list and the pedestrians? Did the officer remain respected as correct but incomplete? What extra graph paper or pre-labelled axes are needed for Lesson 11?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We drew a histogram of the 20 gaps on the 8,000 m stretch of Thika Road with equal 200 m classes (frequencies 5, 9, 0, 2, 1, 3), with bars touching and no bar for the empty class 400 to <600.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: A histogram has touching bars on a continuous axis; with equal class widths the height of a bar shows the frequency. A histogram shows how many values fall in each class, but not where along the road they are.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The histogram shows that most gaps are short (14 of 20 are 300 m or shorter), while a few long gaps of 600 m to 1,100 m lie to the right, and almost none are near the mean of 400 m. So the officer's mean is true but incomplete; the ordered gap list shows the long gaps are in the stretch G9-G14 near the school gate.

LESSONS.title: Unequal Class Widths and Frequency Density
LESSONS.aresKeywords: histogram, frequency density, class width, unequal class width, area represents frequency, gap, Thika Road, long stretch, pedestrians

slo.purpose: Learners merge classes to make unequal class widths, see why frequency cannot be used as the bar height, calculate frequency density and redraw the histogram, then use both histograms to explain where the long gaps and the risk lie.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (d) represent data using histograms with unequal class widths; (e) interpret data from histograms. Unequal-width classes: 0 to <200 (f=5), 200 to <400 (f=9), 400 to <1000 (f=3), 1000 to <1200 (f=3). Frequency density = frequency / class width (in units of 100 m), giving 2.5, 4.5, 0.5, 1.5. Learners know that area represents frequency, and that the tallest bar is the one with the highest frequency density, not the highest frequency.
slo.skills: Calculating frequency density; choosing and labelling scales on both axes; drawing bars that touch with correct boundaries; reading the shape of a histogram; explaining why the tallest bar must be judged by frequency density, not frequency, when widths are unequal; using and interpreting graphs as models (NGSS SEP: Developing and Using Models; Analyzing and Interpreting Data; Constructing Explanations).
slo.attitudes: Core competencies: Critical thinking and problem solving (the learner uses the histograms to examine data and make conclusions); Communication and collaboration. Values: Integrity (the learner records and plots data accurately); Unity (the learner works in groups to draw histograms). PCIs: Life Skills (Decision Making); Road safety. Learners are respectful of the officer, whose mean is true but incomplete.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we represent data? (Also tracked: What is statistics? How do we use statistics in day-to-day life?) Lesson question: What does a histogram of the 20 Thika Road gaps show that the mean of 400 m does not, and why must we use frequency density when class widths are unequal?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 10 drew the equal-width histogram. This lesson merges three classes into one wide class and shows why frequency density is needed; the first time learners meet the idea that area, not height, represents frequency. It also links the histogram evidence to the pedestrians and the near-miss log. Lessons 12 and 13 then draw frequency polygons and compare Thika Road with Mombasa Road.
slo.safetyNotes: The lesson is classroom-based, so no learners go onto the road. If the class revisits the road to check any measurement, this must be done only with Mwalimu Wanjiru and other adults, on the school side of the road, using the designated crossing. Learners must not run across Thika Road to measure anything. Pencils and rulers are used sensibly. Graph paper and charts are shared fairly.

LESSONS.overview: Learners recall the equal-width histogram from Lesson 10. They predict what will happen to the bar if three classes are merged into one wide class: taller or shorter? Then the teacher merges the classes 400 to <600, 600 to <800 and 800 to <1000 into one class, 400 to <1000, holding 3 gaps (600 m, 700 m, 800 m). Learners draw it first with frequency as the height and see a misleading picture, then calculate frequency density (2.5, 4.5, 0.5, 1.5), redraw, and check that bar area represents frequency. In the Explain phase they use both histograms to say why the 400 to <1000 bar is the lowest although it holds 3 gaps, and to link the long stretch G9-G14 to the pedestrians (140 of 182) and the near-miss log (9 of 12). The class updates the DQB and the model. Pacing for a 40-minute period: Predict 4 min, Observe 18 min, Explain 10 min, Driving Question Board 4 min, Model Building 4 min.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the equal-width histogram of the 20 gaps from Lesson 10 in a 1-2 minute recap (frequencies 5, 9, 0, 2, 1, 3). Then they write a prediction: 'If we merge three classes (400 to <600, 600 to <800 and 800 to <1000) into one wide class, will the bar for the merged class be taller or shorter than before? Why?' They share with a partner.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the equal-width table and the merged class. Ask: "If the bars have the same width, what does the height tell us? If one bar is three times wider, what do you think should happen to its height?" Give 1 minute of silent thinking, then WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners. Record 2 predictions on the board without evaluating them.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (prediction stage): learners commit to an idea about height and width before the drawing creates a conflict to resolve.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: whether learners predict that a wider bar should be shorter, or just assume that height equals frequency. Tally how many predict 'taller'; compare later with the real drawing.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4 with graph paper, learners receive the new table: 0 to <200 (f=5), 200 to <400 (f=9), 400 to <1000 (f=3: gaps 600, 700, 800), 1000 to <1200 (f=3). Groups first draw bars with height = frequency and notice that the wide class looks as tall as other bars, and that the picture changes the story. They then calculate frequency density = frequency / class width in units of 100 m: 5/2 = 2.5, 9/2 = 4.5, 3/6 = 0.5, 3/2 = 1.5, and redraw using frequency density on the vertical axis. They shade or count squares to check that bar area represents frequency (for example the first bar: 2.5 high x 2 wide = 5).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Our wide class 400 to <1000 holds 3 gaps: 600 m, 700 m, 800 m. Draw it with height 3 first. What does your picture suggest about gaps between 400 m and 1000 m compared with 200 to <400?" Cold-call 2 groups to share what they see. Then ask: "Is this fair? The class is three times as wide. How could we make the bar height fair?" Introduce frequency density only after learners voice the problem: "Frequency density = frequency divided by class width, with width in units of 100 m." Circulate, check scales and that each group has 2.5, 4.5, 0.5 and 1.5. Ask one group to count squares to show area = frequency. Provide pre-labelled axes for learners who need support.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Productive Struggle with Cognitive Conflict: the frequency-height drawing of the wide class creates a visible conflict (it seems to say gaps of 400 m to 1000 m are common), and frequency density resolves it. Gallery Walk and Modelling: learners compare drawn graphs, building an abstract idea (area represents frequency) from concrete bars.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) bars touch and have correct boundaries on the continuous axis; (2) frequency densities calculated correctly as 2.5, 4.5, 0.5, 1.5; (3) the wide bar 400 to <1000 is drawn at height 0.5, the lowest bar; (4) axes labelled 'Gap length (m)' and 'Frequency density'. Note groups who divide by 600 instead of 6 (the unit error) and prompt: "What unit are we using for class width?" Exit-check: 3 cold-called learners state the units.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners use both histograms to explain the phenomenon. In groups they answer: (1) In the unequal-width histogram, why is the bar for 400 to <1000 the lowest although it holds 3 gaps, the same as 1000 to <1200 (also 3 gaps)? (2) The long stretch G9-G14 (identified from the ordered gap list) holds 140 of the 182 undesignated crossers (77%) and 9 of the 12 near-misses (75%). What does the histogram add to this? (3) How does this show why the mean of 400 m is true but incomplete? They write a 3-sentence explanation: 'The histogram shows... The mean hides this because... Pedestrians are at risk in...'
framework.teacherMoves: Ask learners to explain frequency density to a partner in one sentence: "A tall bar of high density means gaps packed closely in that range, not just many gaps." Cold-call 3 pairs. Correct the misconception that the tallest bar is always the highest frequency when widths are unequal: the tallest bar is the highest frequency density. Then ask: "Which bar shows the gaps of 1,000 m, 1,050 m and 1,100 m? Which gaps on the road are those?" WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 learners. Say: "Ms Halima Abdi is not wrong; her mean is correct but incomplete. What does the picture add?" Make the distinction explicit again: the histogram shows HOW MANY gaps are long; the ordered gap list and the pedestrian counts show WHERE the danger is. Do not re-teach mean or median calculation.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with Talk Moves: learners make a claim about where the danger lies, support it with the histogram, and reason using frequency density. Revoicing and 'add on' talk moves build a shared explanation that connects the graph to the phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for: (1) learners using 'frequency density' and 'class width' accurately; (2) the idea that area represents frequency; (3) linking the long gaps to the long stretch G9-G14 with the numbers 5,250 m, 140 of 182 pedestrians and 9 of 12 near-misses. Collect the 3-sentence explanations and sort into: describes shape only / links to the mean / links to pedestrian risk. Plan a short revisit of any group still saying the tallest bar is always the most frequent.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class DQB. They add sticky notes: new answers or evidence for the key inquiry questions (What is statistics? How do we represent data? How do we use statistics in day-to-day life?) and new questions arising, such as 'How can we show the gap pattern as a line graph to compare Thika Road with Mombasa Road?' or 'Which crossing points should be added first?' They move or mark questions answered by today's histograms, for example 'How do we represent data?' now has the evidence 'histograms with equal and unequal widths, using frequency density'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Take 2 minutes silently to write one thing the histogram taught you and one new question. Then place your note on the DQB." WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before inviting the first learner. Cold-call 3 learners to read a note and say which key inquiry question it connects to. Ask: "Which question on our board did today's evidence help us answer? Which still needs data?" Point out that Lesson 12 will draw frequency polygons and compare Thika Road with Mombasa Road. Group similar questions and highlight one that connects to the community presentation in Lesson 15.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a public record of learning: sorting questions into answered, partly answered and open shows learners how today's evidence moves the class understanding forward and sustains motivation for the next lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that notes are specific (for example mention frequency density or the wide class) rather than generic. Count how many learners connect a note to one of the 3 KICD key inquiry questions. Note learners whose questions still reflect the 'mean = safe' idea and plan to address them in Lesson 12 and Lesson 14.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise the class model of the phenomenon (a poster or diagram on a chart). They add a sketch of the histogram and annotate: 'Most gaps are short (14 of 20 are 300 m or shorter). A few very long gaps (600 m to 1,100 m) sit to the right and pull the mean up to 400 m. These long gaps are in the long stretch G9-G14, 5,250 m, with the school gate.' They add the rule: 'With unequal class widths, compare frequency density, not frequency.' They then complete their summary table row for this lesson.
framework.teacherMoves: Ask: "What can we now add to our model that we could not show in Lessons 8 and 9?" WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to propose one addition each and ask the class to agree or add on. Prompt: "Which part of the histogram best shows the danger near the school gate? What would you say to Ms Halima Abdi and Mzee Otieno using this graph?" Remind learners that this is a one-morning sample (Tuesday, 6:30-7:30 am) and should be repeated. Link ahead: "Next lesson we will draw frequency polygons and compare with Mombasa Road." Collect one model annotation per group.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision: adding the histogram to the model makes the graph a tool for explanation, not just a drawing. Learners must say what the model can now explain (where the long gaps are) and what it cannot yet (comparison with another road).
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: the revised model (1) names the shape (short gaps cluster plus long gaps to the right), (2) states that the mean of 400 m is true but incomplete, (3) mentions the long stretch G9-G14 and the 20-gap sample from Thika Road, and (4) states the frequency density rule. Use a 3-point check (missing, partial, complete) on each group's poster. Ask one learner to explain what density 0.5 for 400 to <1000 means.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: Which groups divided by the class width in metres instead of units of 100 m? Did the wide class genuinely create cognitive conflict, and did frequency density make sense to learners as 'squeezing' a wide class to a fair height? Which learners can read the histogram but cannot yet link it to the pedestrians and the near-miss log? Did the officer remain respected as correct but incomplete? What extra graph paper or pre-labelled axes are needed for Lesson 12?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We merged three classes into 400 to <1000 and found that using frequency as the bar height was misleading. Frequency density gave 2.5, 4.5, 0.5 and 1.5, and we redrew the histogram of the 20 gaps on the 8,000 m stretch of Thika Road.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: A histogram has touching bars on a continuous axis, and bar area represents frequency. Frequency density = frequency / class width (in units of 100 m). With unequal class widths, the tallest bar is the one with the highest frequency density, not the highest frequency.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The histogram shows that most gaps are short (14 of 20 are 300 m or shorter), while a few long gaps of 600 m to 1,100 m lie to the right. These long gaps pull the mean up to 400 m and sit in the long stretch G9-G14 near the school gate. So the officer's mean is true but incomplete: the histogram shows how the gap lengths are spread, and the ordered gap list and pedestrian counts show where along the road the risk is.

LESSONS.title: Frequency Polygons by Hand: Plotting Midpoints and Closing the Polygon
LESSONS.aresKeywords: frequency polygon, midpoint, class, closing the polygon, hump, tail, spread, Thika Road

slo.purpose: Learners draw the Thika Road frequency polygon by hand from the grouped table, plotting (midpoint, frequency) points, closing the polygon on the axis, and reading its shape (modal class, dip, small rise and tail).
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (1) plot (midpoint, frequency) points from a grouped table and join them with straight lines; (2) close the polygon on the horizontal axis at both ends; (3) interpret the polygon (modal class, dips, humps and tails). KICD outcomes: d) represent data using histograms and frequency polygons; e) interpret data from histograms and frequency polygons.
slo.skills: Plotting points on a scale; using midpoints from the grouped table; using a spreadsheet to build a scatter or line chart; comparing graphs. NGSS-aligned practices: Analyzing and Interpreting Data; Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking; Developing and Using Models; Engaging in Argument from Evidence. KICD core competencies: Critical thinking and problem solving (uses frequency polygons to examine data and make conclusions); Digital literacy (uses digital devices to draw frequency polygons); Communication and collaboration.
slo.attitudes: KICD values: Integrity (plots and records data accurately); Unity (works in groups using collected data to draw frequency polygons). PCIs: Life Skills (Decision Making), as learners make informed decisions from the polygons; Road safety, as learners discuss where pedestrians are at risk. Learners respect Ms Halima Abdi's mean as correct but incomplete.
slo.keyInquiry: KICD key inquiry questions: 1. What is statistics? 2. How do we represent data? 3. How do we use statistics in day-to-day life? This lesson focuses on question 2 (How do we represent data?) and moves towards question 3.
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 7 gave the classes, Lessons 8 and 9 the midpoints, and Lessons 10 and 11 the skill of reading shape from histograms. This lesson turns the same grouped table into a frequency polygon by hand. Lesson 13 then repeats it with a spreadsheet and puts a second road on the same axes, so that two roads can be compared.
slo.safetyNotes: Learners work indoors with graph paper, rulers and sharp pencils; keep pencils and compasses stored when not in use. Phones and school computers: charge in advance, keep cables out of walkways, and share devices fairly. No roadside work in this lesson. If any learner refers to the real Thika Road, remind the class that the data come from a morning count taken with adult supervision and that learners must never cross at undesignated spots themselves.

LESSONS.overview: Back at Ruaraka Hills Secondary School on Thika Road, Mwalimu Wanjiru reminds the class that Ms Halima Abdi's mean of 400 m is correct but incomplete, and that Mzee Otieno's log places 9 of 12 near-misses in one stretch. Learners first predict what a line graph of the Thika Road gap data (20 gaps, classes of width 200 m) will look like and which class will have the highest point. They then draw the polygon by hand on graph paper from the midpoints (100, 300, 500, 700, 900, 1100) and frequencies (5, 9, 0, 2, 1, 3), closing it at (-100, 0) and (1300, 0). In the Explain phase they read its shape and compare it with the histogram from Lesson 10: the same data, shown as a line. The class updates the DQB and the model. The spreadsheet version and the road comparison follow in Lesson 13. Pacing for a 40-minute period: Predict 4 min, Observe 17 min, Explain 10 min, Driving Question Board 4 min, Model Building 5 min.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the officer's claim and Mzee Otieno's remark in a 1-2 minute recap. Individually, in 2 minutes, they sketch what they think a line graph of the Thika Road gap data would look like (20 gaps in 6 classes of width 200 m) and write a prediction: 'The highest point will be at ... because ...' They share in pairs. Sketches are kept for comparison at the end of the lesson.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Ms Halima Abdi's 400 m is correct but incomplete. Today we draw a picture that shows what the average hides.' Display the grouped table (classes 0 to <200, 200 to <400, 400 to <600, 600 to <800, 800 to <1000, 1000 to <1200 with frequencies 5, 9, 0, 2, 1, 3). Ask: 'Without calculating anything, which class do you expect to have the highest point on a line graph, and why?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners, including at least 1 who has not spoken today, with 'Achieng, what did your partner predict?' Do not correct predictions yet; write 3 different predictions on the board.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (prediction stage): committing to a prediction in writing exposes learners' ideas, so that the polygon creates something to test.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether sketches show a peak at the 200 to <400 class and whether learners expect a dip at the empty class. Note learners who mention the long gaps or the school gate unprompted.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4 with graph paper, learners use the Thika Road grouped table from earlier lessons. Kiprop-style table-keepers write the midpoints (100, 300, 500, 700, 900, 1100) next to the frequencies (5, 9, 0, 2, 1, 3). Njeri-style graphers choose scales (horizontal axis from -100 to 1300 m, vertical axis 0 to 10), plot the six points, then add (-100, 0) and (1300, 0) and join all eight points with straight lines using a ruler. They label the axes ('Gap between crossing points (m)' and 'Frequency') and give a title. They check that both ends of the polygon lie on the horizontal axis.
framework.teacherMoves: Model the first two points on the board: 'The midpoint of 0 to <200 is (0 + 200)/2 = 100, so our first point is (100, 5).' Circulate and ask: 'Why do we plot at the midpoint and not at the class boundary?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Ask: 'Why do we close the polygon at -100 and 1300?' and cold-call 3 groups. Prompt with 'What is the frequency of the class 400 to <600 on Thika Road? So where does the line go?' (the line drops to the axis at (500, 0)). Check scales: 'Does your 1100 m point fit on your axis?' Remind: 'Say Thika Road, the unit in metres and the 20-gap sample when you quote any figure.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data representation and modelling: translating a table into a graph by hand lets learners see how the same numbers produce shape, and plotting at midpoints connects the polygon to the earlier midpoint work.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each group's polygon: eight points on Thika Road ((-100,0), (100,5), (300,9), (500,0), (700,2), (900,1), (1100,3), (1300,0)); points at midpoints, not boundaries; straight lines with a ruler; closed at both ends; labelled axes. Note groups that join the last point to the axis incorrectly, or that miss the zero-frequency class.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups answer in writing: (1) Where is the highest point of the polygon, and what does it tell us? (The modal class 200 to <400.) (2) What happens at 500 m? (The line drops to 0: the empty class 400 to <600.) (3) Describe the right-hand end: a small rise at 1100 (3 gaps in 1000 to <1200) after the dip. (4) Compare the polygon with the histogram from Lesson 10: what is the same and what is different? (The same data; the polygon joins midpoints with straight lines instead of showing bars.) They write one sentence: 'The officer's claim is true but incomplete because the polygon shows ...' and link it to the long stretch G9-G14 (5,250 m, 140 of 182 pedestrians, 9 of 12 near-misses).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at your polygon silently for 1 minute and write down 2 things it shows.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 4 groups and push for evidence: 'Which points on the graph show that?' Ask: 'Where is the 400 m mean on your polygon? Is that where most gaps are?' Press: 'The polygon shows how many gaps are long. Which of our lists tells us where along the road the long gaps are?' (the ordered gap list G1-G20: G9-G14.) Remind learners that grouped means are estimates (the true Thika Road mean is 400 m) and that this is a one-morning sample. Reinforce the language: 'The officer's claim is true but incomplete.' Never say 'wrong'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning: learners make a claim about what the polygon shows, support it with specific points on the graph, and compare two representations of the same data.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for statements that use evidence such as 'the line drops to 0 at 500' and 'a small rise at 1100'. Check the sentence frame for the phrases 'true but incomplete' and 'estimate'. Mark learners who think the polygon shows WHERE on the road the gaps are. Note use of units (m) and the 20-gap sample.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board. Individually they write on sticky notes: (a) one answer they can now give, with evidence from today's polygon; (b) one new question. Examples: 'Would the polygon look the same on another road?' 'Would the polygon change on a Saturday?' 'Can a computer draw the polygon for us?' Notes are placed under the three KICD questions: What is statistics? How do we represent data? How do we use statistics in day-to-day life?
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Go to our DQB. Which question can we now answer using today's polygon?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to place a note and say why. Highlight any question about comparing roads or using a computer and park it for Lesson 13. Praise respectful questions about the officer: 'Good statisticians question the data, not the person.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board: sorting questions under the three KICD key inquiry questions makes progress visible and keeps the investigation learner-driven.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that notes include evidence from the polygon (not just opinions), that they are placed under the correct KICD question, and that some questions go beyond today (comparing roads, repeating counts).

framework.learnerExperience: Learners update the class model of the phenomenon, a diagram or concept map with the officer's claim at the centre. They add (1) the frequency polygon shape for Thika Road with its dip at 500 m and small rise at 1100 m; (2) a link to the histogram: the same data in a different picture; and (3) a connection to the long stretch G9-G14 near the school gate where 140 of 182 pedestrians and 9 of 12 near-misses occurred. Each group adds one arrow and one sentence and notes one limitation (one-morning sample, grouped estimates).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model needs a new piece today. What does the polygon add that the mean could not show?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups for their added arrow and sentence. Ask: 'How does this connect to Mzee Otieno's log of 12 near-misses, with 9 in the long stretch?' Hand-off: 'Next lesson we draw the polygon with a spreadsheet and put Mombasa Road on the same axes.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision: adding the polygon layer shows learners how each representation (table, mean, histogram, polygon) contributes a different part of the explanation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: the polygon is added with the dip and the rise; the link to the long stretch is made; a limitation is stated. Sort the models into three piles (secure, nearly there, needs reteaching of midpoints or closing the polygon) to plan Lesson 13 groupings.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson ask yourself: (1) Did every group close the polygon at -100 and 1300 and plot at midpoints, and which groups confused boundaries with midpoints? (2) Did learners see that the polygon and histogram show the same data? (3) Which learners think the polygon shows where along the road the gaps are? (4) Did learners keep to 'true but incomplete' language about the officer's claim? Note names and plan small support groups for Lesson 13.

summaryTablePrompt.learned: A frequency polygon plots (midpoint, frequency), joins the points with straight lines and is closed on the axis at both ends. It shows the same data as the histogram, as a line.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The officer's claim is true but incomplete. The polygon shows a peak at 200 to <400, a dip to zero at 400 to <600 where the mean of 400 m falls, and a small rise at 1000 to <1200, so one average cannot show the shape of the gaps. This is one morning's sample and should be repeated.

LESSONS.title: Spreadsheet Polygons and Comparing Roads: Same Mean, Different Shape
LESSONS.aresKeywords: frequency polygon, midpoint, spreadsheet, closing the polygon, hump, tail, spread, comparison, Thika Road, Mombasa Road

slo.purpose: Learners draw frequency polygons with a spreadsheet or digital device, add the Mombasa Road (Embakasi stretch) data on the same axes, and compare the two polygons to show that similar averages can hide different spread.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (1) draw a frequency polygon with a spreadsheet or digital device and check it against the hand-drawn one; (2) compare two polygons from different roads and make a conclusion supported by data; (3) explain why similar means (Thika Road 440 m, Mombasa Road 380 m, both grouped estimates) can hide different shapes. KICD outcomes: d) represent data using histograms and frequency polygons; e) interpret data from histograms and frequency polygons. Core competency: Digital literacy.
slo.skills: Plotting points on a scale; using midpoints from the grouped table; using a spreadsheet to build a scatter or line chart; comparing graphs. NGSS-aligned practices: Analyzing and Interpreting Data; Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking; Developing and Using Models; Engaging in Argument from Evidence. KICD core competencies: Critical thinking and problem solving (uses frequency polygons to examine data and make conclusions); Digital literacy (uses digital devices to draw frequency polygons); Communication and collaboration.
slo.attitudes: KICD values: Integrity (plots and records data accurately); Unity (works in groups using collected data to draw frequency polygons). PCIs: Life Skills (Decision Making), as learners make informed decisions from the polygons; Road safety, as learners discuss where pedestrians are at risk. Learners respect Ms Halima Abdi's mean as correct but incomplete.
slo.keyInquiry: KICD key inquiry questions: 1. What is statistics? 2. How do we represent data? 3. How do we use statistics in day-to-day life? This lesson focuses on question 2 (How do we represent data?) and moves towards question 3.
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 12 drew the Thika Road polygon by hand. This lesson repeats it digitally and compares two roads on one set of axes. It shows that the Thika Road mean (grouped estimate 440 m) and the Mombasa Road mean (380 m) are similar, yet the shapes differ: Thika Road has a second small rise at 1000 to <1200 m. This gives the evidence for Lesson 14, where learners make their final interpretation.
slo.safetyNotes: Learners work indoors with graph paper, rulers and sharp pencils; keep pencils and compasses stored when not in use. Phones and school computers: charge in advance, keep cables out of walkways, and share devices fairly. No roadside work in this lesson. If any learner refers to the real Thika Road, remind the class that the data come from a morning count taken with adult supervision and that learners must never cross at undesignated spots themselves.

LESSONS.overview: Learners recall the Thika Road polygon from Lesson 12 and predict whether two roads with similar means will have similar graphs. Groups then enter midpoints and frequencies into a spreadsheet, insert a line or scatter-with-lines chart for Thika Road, add a second column of Mombasa Road Embakasi frequencies (4, 8, 5, 2, 1, 0) so both polygons appear on the same axes, and check that the Mombasa Road grouped mean is 380 m (7,600/20). Groups without devices draw both polygons on one sheet using two colours. In the Explain phase they compare hump, tail and spread, and conclude that similar means (440 m and 380 m) hide different shapes: Thika Road has a second small rise at 1000 to <1200 m, while Mombasa Road has no gap of 1000 m or more. The class updates the DQB and the cumulative model, and an exit slip checks each learner's reasoning. Pacing for a 40-minute period: Predict 4 min, Observe 16 min, Explain 10 min, Driving Question Board 4 min, Model Building 6 min.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the hand-drawn Thika Road polygon from Lesson 12 in a 1-2 minute recap. Individually in 2 minutes they write a prediction: 'Mombasa Road has a grouped mean of 380 m and Thika Road 440 m. Will their graphs look alike? Why or why not?' They share in pairs, then with the class. Their predictions are kept for comparison at the end of the lesson.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Ms Halima Abdi's 400 m is correct but incomplete. Today we compare two roads.' Ask: 'If two roads have similar means, should their graphs be similar? Raise a hand for yes, no, not sure.' Record the counts. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners, including at least 2 who have not spoken today. Do not correct predictions yet; write 3 different predictions on the board.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (prediction stage): committing to a prediction in writing exposes learners' ideas that the mean describes the whole data set, so the later comparison of polygons creates a genuine conflict to resolve.
framework.formativeAssessment: Tally the yes/no/not sure counts. Look for the misconception that equal means imply equal graphs. Note learners who mention the long gaps or the school gate unprompted.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups, with a spreadsheet or phone (about 16 minutes), groups enter midpoints in one column and frequencies in another, insert a line or scatter-with-lines chart, and add a second column of Mombasa Road frequencies (4, 8, 5, 2, 1, 0) so both polygons appear on the same axes. They label axes ('Gap between crossing points (m)' and 'Frequency'), give a title, and check that both polygons are closed at -100 and 1300. Learners also confirm the Mombasa Road grouped mean: 400 + 2400 + 2500 + 1400 + 900 + 0 = 7,600, and 7,600/20 = 380 m. Groups without devices draw both polygons on one sheet using two colours. They compare the spreadsheet chart with the hand-drawn polygon from Lesson 12.
framework.teacherMoves: Show the steps on the teacher device and let group leaders lead. Support device-sharing: rotate who types every 4 minutes. Circulate and ask: 'Do both polygons start and end on the axis?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Prompt: 'Does your spreadsheet chart match your hand-drawn polygon? If not, which one is right, and how do you check?' Ask groups to check the Mombasa Road grouped mean by hand. Remind: 'Say Thika Road or Mombasa Road, the unit in metres and the 20-gap sample when you quote any figure.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data Representation and Modelling: translating a table into a graph with a spreadsheet and checking it against the hand-drawn polygon builds trust in both methods (Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking).
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each group's chart: Thika Road points (-100,0), (100,5), (300,9), (500,0), (700,2), (900,1), (1100,3), (1300,0); Mombasa Road points (100,4), (300,8), (500,5), (700,2), (900,1), (1100,0); labelled axes; both closed. Ask 2 learners to explain the spreadsheet chart. Record how many groups verify 380 m correctly.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups place the two polygons side by side or on one chart and complete a comparison frame: (1) Where is the highest point on each road? (2) How many classes have gaps of 600 m or more, and how many gaps? (3) Describe the right-hand end of each graph. (4) What do the means 440 m (Thika Road, grouped estimate) and 380 m (Mombasa Road) tell us, and what do they hide? Learners notice that both have a modal class of 200 to <400, but Thika Road has a dip to 0 at 400 to <600, a small rise at 1000 to <1200 (3 gaps), and reaches a longer tail, while Mombasa Road is a single hump with a short right tail, its longest gap in 800 to <1000, and no gap of 1000 m or more. They write one sentence: 'The officer's claim is true but incomplete because ...', using the polygon, and link it to the long stretch G9-G14 (5,250 m, 140 of 182 pedestrians, 9 of 12 near-misses). They then compare their Predict-phase sketches with the real polygons and revise their ideas.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Put the two polygons next to each other. Silently look for 1 minute and write down 2 differences and 1 similarity.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. Ask: 'Both roads have the same modal class, 200 to <400. What is different?' Cold-call 5 groups and push for evidence: 'Which points on the graph show that?' Ask: 'Thika Road and Mombasa Road have similar means, 440 m and 380 m. If you were a pedestrian, would you feel equally safe on both? Use the polygons to argue.' Take 2 competing arguments before revealing a view. Press: 'The polygon shows how many gaps are long. Which of our lists tells us where along the road the long gaps are?' (the ordered gap list G1-G20: G9-G14, with the school gate inside G11, the 1,100 m gap). The right-hand part of the polygon (600 m upwards) shows how many long gaps there are, not where they lie. Add: 'A polygon shows shape, but remember this is one weekday morning on 20 gaps. How should we describe our confidence?' Reinforce the language: 'The officer's claim is true but incomplete.' Never say 'wrong'. Remind learners that grouped means are estimates (the true Thika Road mean is 400 m).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Comparing Models / Argument from Evidence (Claim-Evidence-Reasoning): learners make a claim about the two roads, support it with specific points on the polygons, and reason about why the means hide the difference in spread. Comparison forces attention to shape, the idea the mean cannot show.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for statements that use evidence such as 'Thika Road has 3 gaps in 1000 to <1200 but Mombasa Road has none', and for the correct idea that similar means can hide different spread. Check the sentence frame for the phrases 'true but incomplete' and 'estimate'. Mark learners who still say the graphs should look the same because the means are close. Note use of units (m) and the 20-gap sample.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board started in Lesson 1. Individually they write on sticky notes: (a) one answer they can now give, with evidence from today's polygons; (b) one new question. Examples: 'Why does Mombasa Road have no gap of 1000 m or more?' 'Would the polygon change on a Saturday?' 'How can a polygon help the county decide where to put a footbridge?' Notes are placed under the three KICD questions: What is statistics? How do we represent data? How do we use statistics in day-to-day life? The class moves the questions about drawing frequency polygons and comparing roads to 'answered', and keeps those about recommendations for Lesson 15.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Go to our DQB. Which question can we now answer using today's polygons?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners to place a note and say why: 'Njeri, which question is this, and what is your evidence?' Ask: 'Which of our new questions can only be answered by taking more data, for example repeating the count on another day?' Highlight any question about what to recommend and park it for Lesson 15. Praise respectful questions about the officer: 'Good statisticians question the data, not the person.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board: sorting questions under the three KICD key inquiry questions makes progress visible and keeps the investigation learner-driven, linking today's polygons to the larger puzzle of how an average can say the road is safe while the data show danger.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that notes include evidence from the polygons (not just opinions), that they are placed under the correct KICD question, and that at least some questions go beyond today (repeat counts, recommendations). Note learners who write only 'polygons show shape' and prompt them to say what the shape shows about the road.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners update the class model of the phenomenon, a diagram or concept map with the officer's claim at the centre. They add: (1) the frequency polygon shape for Thika Road with its second rise at 1000 to <1200 m; (2) the Mombasa Road polygon as a comparison with a shorter tail; (3) a new link: 'similar means (440 m and 380 m) can hide different spread, so we need to look at the polygon as well as the average'; (4) a connection to the long stretch G9-G14 near the school gate where 140 of 182 pedestrians and 9 of 12 near-misses occurred. Each group adds one arrow and one sentence and notes one limitation (one-morning sample, grouped estimates).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model needs a new piece today. What does the polygon add that the mean could not show?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups for their added arrow and sentence. Ask: 'How does this connect to Mzee Otieno's log of 12 near-misses, with 9 in the long stretch?' Ask: 'What would you want to check on the polygon before telling the Parents Association or the county roads office?' Close with an exit slip, to be answered individually in 3 minutes: 'In two sentences, explain why the Thika Road and Mombasa Road means are similar but the polygons are not. Give one number from each road.' Collect the slips. Preview Lesson 14: 'Next time we put everything together and make recommendations.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision: adding the polygon layer shows learners how each representation (table, mean, histogram, polygon) contributes a different part of the explanation, and the exit slip makes each learner's reasoning visible.
framework.formativeAssessment: Exit slip indicators: correctly states that both means are similar (440 m and 380 m, grouped estimates) while Thika Road has a second rise at 1000 to <1200 m or a longer right tail; uses numbers and units; uses 'true but incomplete' language; mentions that the sample is one morning. Sort slips into three piles (secure, nearly there, needs reteaching of midpoints or closing the polygon) to plan Lesson 14 groupings.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson ask yourself: (1) Did the spreadsheet help or distract, and did every learner get a turn at the device? (2) Did learners compare shape (humps, tails, spread) or only compare means? (3) Which learners still believe that equal means imply equal data? (4) Did learners keep to 'true but incomplete' language about the officer's claim? (5) What will you adjust in Lesson 14 for learners who struggled with scales or with using evidence in a claim? Note names and plan small support groups.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We drew the Thika Road frequency polygon (20 gaps, classes of width 200 m) and the Mombasa Road (Embakasi) polygon with frequencies 4, 8, 5, 2, 1, 0 on the same axes, with a spreadsheet and by hand.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Putting two polygons on the same axes lets us compare their shape and spread. The grouped means are similar (Thika Road 440 m, Mombasa Road 380 m) and both have the modal class 200 to <400.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The officer's claim is true but incomplete. Similar averages can hide different shapes: Thika Road has a second small rise at 1000 to <1200 m and long gaps, while Mombasa Road is a single hump with no gap of 1000 m or more. One average cannot show where pedestrians are at risk, so we use the polygon together with the median, mode and the long stretch G9-G14. This is one morning's sample and should be repeated.
